also admitted that as per policy conditions, in cases of death due
to motor vehicle accident, the Insurance Company is liable to pay
13
compensation unless there is a breach of policy conditions.

12. No breach of policy has been proved in the present case.  It is
also relevant to note that in Sessions Trial No. 125/2010, the
learned Additional Sessions Judge, South Bastar, Dantewada,
after appreciating the entire evidence including the medical
evidence, post-mortem report, and forensic examination of the
vehicles, recorded a clear finding that the prosecution failed to
prove the charges of murder and criminal conspiracy and
accordingly acquitted the accused persons. The criminal Court
found that the condition of the vehicles was such that the incident
could be the result of an accident. This finding strongly supports
the case of the appellants.  Merely because the family members
of the deceased had initially expressed suspicion regarding
murder, the same cannot override the consistent ocular, medical
and documentary evidence pointing towards an accidental death.
The Tribunal appears to have been unduly influenced by such
stray doubts expressed by the widow of the deceased, while
ignoring the cogent testimony of the independent eye-witness and
other reliable evidence on record.

13. The learned Tribunal also erred in discarding the testimony of
Mukesh Kumar Kashyap (A.W.-2) without any cogent reason. On
a holistic appreciation of the entire evidence, his testimony
inspires confidence and is fully corroborated by medical and
documentary evidence. The finding of the Tribunal that the death
was not caused due to rash and negligent driving of the offending
14
vehicle is, therefore, erroneous and unsustainable in law.

14. This Court is further fortified by the principles laid down by the
Division Bench of this Court in United India Insurance Company
Limited, Raipur vs. Rani Solanki and Others, MAC No.
182/2013 decided on 14.08.2020, wherein it has been held that
once the criminal charge of murder does not stand proved and is
set aside, the liability under the Motor Vehicles Act would revive,
provided the incident is otherwise established as an accident. It
was held thus :
“11. Coming to the scope for payment
of compensation under the MV Act and
the coverage of third party risk, Chapter
XI has been provided for insurance of
the motor vehicles against the third
party risk. Section 146 speaks about
the necessity for insurance against third
party risk to the effect that no person
shall use, except as a passenger, or
cause or allow any other person to use,
a motor vehicle in a public place, unless
there is in force in relation to the use of
the vehicle by that person or that other
person, as the case may be, a policy of
insurance
 
complying
 
with
 
the
requirements of the said Chapter. The
requirements of policy and limits of
liability have been mentioned under
Section 147 of the MV Act; whereas the
duty of the insurers to satisfy judgments
against persons insured in respect of
third party risk has been dealt with
under Section 149 of the MV Act.

12. As mentioned already, on
occurrence of an accident involving use
of a motor vehicle, compensation can
be claimed either under Section 163A
15
of the MV Act on the basis of a
structured formula (where it is not
necessary for the Claimants to plead or
prove negligence on the part of the
Driver or the Owner) or under Section
166 of the MV Act by proving the
negligence on the part of the Driver of
the offending vehicle. It is quite possible
that in a given case, 'murder' can be an
'accident'. If only it amounts to an
'accident', can it lead to a claim petition,
to be filed by the Claimants, seeking
compensation in respect of such
accident because of the use of the
motor vehicle either under Section
163A or under Section 166 of the MV
Act. The Claims Tribunal envisaged
under Section 165 of the MV Act names
the Tribunal as 'Motor Accidents Claims
Tribunal' and if it is not an accident, no
such claim can be held as
maintainable, to be entertained by the
Tribunal.

13. The question whether a murder can
be an accident in a given case had
come up for consideration before the
Apex Court in Rita Devi (supra). It was
a case where some unknown
passengers hired an Autorickshaw from
an autostand at Dimapur and later, the
vehicle was reported stolen and the
dead body of the Driver was recovered
by the Police on the next day. The
Autorickshaw was never recovered and
the claim of the owner for the loss of
Autorickshaw was considered and
sanctioned by the Insurer, satisfying the
amount for which it was settled. A claim
petition was filed by the legal
representatives of the deceased Driver
under Section 163A of the MV Act,
claiming compensation for the death as
having arisen out of and in the course
16
of his employment. The Tribunal held
that it was caused by 'accident' coming
within the purview of the MV Act and
the owner and the Insurer were liable.
The Insurance Company took up the
matter before the High Court where it
was held that there was no motor
accident as contemplated under the MV
Act and that it was an act of murder.
Accordingly, the appeal was allowed
and the award passed by the Tribunal
was set aside. This led to the
proceedings before the Apex Court
where the question was subjected to a
threadbare analysis; particularly on the
point of 'dominant intention'. The Apex
Court observed that there are instances
where murder can be by accident on a
given set of facts and that the
difference between a murder 'which is
not an accident' and a murder 'which is
an accident' depends upon the
proximity of the cause of murder. The
Apex Court held that if the 'dominant
intention' of the act of felony is to kill
any particular person, then such killing
is not an accidental murder but a
'murder simplicitor'; whereas, in a case
where act of murder was originally not
intended and the same was caused in
furtherance of any other felonious act,
then such murder is an 'accidental
murder'.”

15. Applying the aforesaid principle to the facts of the present case,
there remains no doubt that the death of the deceased was
accidental.  Now, coming to the facts and circumstances of the
present case in light of the evidence and settled legal position, this
Court has no hesitation in holding that the deceased Lachhu
Karma died due to injuries sustained in a motor accident caused
17
by rash and negligent driving of the offending Commander Jeep
by respondent No. 1. The finding of the Tribunal to the contrary is
liable to be set aside.

16. It is also pertinent to note that the learned Tribunal had already
assessed the compensation payable to the appellants at
Rs. 37,56,720/-, but declined to award the same solely on the
erroneous premise that the death was not accidental. Once this
premise is found to be incorrect, the appellants are entitled to
compensation as determined.

17. Consequently, the impugned judgment and award dated
30.01.2017 passed by the learned Additional Motor Accident
Claims Tribunal, Fast Track Court, South Bastar, Dantewada
(C.G.), in Claim Case No. 156/2014 is hereby set aside.  It is held
that the deceased Lachhu Karma died due to a motor accident
that occurred on 03.04.2010 involving the offending Commander
Jeep bearing registration No. C.G. 07 ZD-2925, which was being
driven by respondent No. 1 in a rash and negligent manner.

18. Having held that the appellants/claimants are entitled to
compensation, this Court further finds it necessary to examine
whether the compensation assessed by the learned Tribunal is
just and proper. The Tribunal had calculated the compensation to
the tune of Rs. 37,56,720/-. However, from a perusal of the
record, it appears that the Tribunal has not properly assessed the
compensation under the conventional heads.

19. The claimants are entitled for Rs. 18,000/- towards loss of estate
18
(increase of 10% in every three years) and Rs. 18,000/- for
funeral expenses (increase of 10% in every three years). As per
'Magma General Insurance Co. Ltd., the claimants are further
entitled for Rs. (40,000/-X4+10%+10%) each (with increase of
10% in every three years) i.e. Rs. 1,92,000/- for consortium.
Accordingly, the appellants/claimants would become entitled for
total compensation of Rs. 37,14,720/- in the following manner:-

21. It is further held that respondent No. 3, the Insurance Company, is

1.
The contents and factual matrix involved in all the writ petitions
would revel that the bone of contention in them is one and the
same, as such, all these writ petitions are clubbed together, heard
together and are being decided by this common order.

2.
Writ petition No. 482 of 2023 has been taken as lead case in order
to decide the issues involved in this matter. The petitioner in the
said writ petition has prayed for following reliefs :- 
“10.1 That, this Hon'ble Court may kindly be
pleased to direct the respondents to produce
the entire records of the case pertaining to the
Services of the petitioners.  
10.2 That, this Hon'ble Court may kindly be
pleased to direct the respondents to regularize
the services of the petitioners with the
Municipal Corporation, Bilaspur. 12  
10.3 That, this Hon'ble Court may kindly be
pleased to direct the respondents to pay
regular pay scale to the petitioners.  
8
10.4 Any other relief(s)/ order(s)/ direction(s)
in favour of petitioner, which this Hon'ble Court
may deem fit and proper in the facts and
circumstances of the case, in the interest of
justice.  
10.5 Cost of the petition.”

3.
Brief facts of the case, as projected by the petitioner, are that the
respondent No.1 is the State of Chhattisgarh and respondent
No.2 is an officer functioning under the administrative control of
respondent No.1. Respondent No.3 is a statutory body
incorporated under the provisions of the Chhattisgarh Municipal
Corporation Act, 1956 (hereinafter referred to as “the Act, 1956”
for the sake of brevity), and respondent No.4 is an officer of
respondent No.3. Respondent Nos.5 to 7 are independent
contractors engaged by respondent No.4 for execution of
municipal works. Thus, all the respondents are either the State or
its instrumentalities within the meaning of Article 12 of the
Constitution of India and are amenable to the writ jurisdiction of
this Court.  The petitioners are presently working on the post of
Cleaning Supervisor. They were initially appointed by different
Gram Panchayats/Nagar Panchayats, as per the local
requirements, on different dates. Petitioner No.1 was appointed
on 12.08.2016 by Gram Panchayat Mopka; Petitioner Nos.2 and 3
were appointed on 01.11.2008 by Nagar Panchayat Sakri;
Petitioner No.4 was appointed on 25.01.2019 by Gram Panchayat
Devrikhurd; and Petitioner No.5 was appointed on 24.11.2015 by
9
Gram Panchayat Khamtarai. Since their initial appointments, the
petitioners have been continuously discharging their duties
sincerely and to the satisfaction of the authorities. Owing to their
satisfactory performance and requirement of work, their services
were extended from time to time by issuing fresh
appointment/extension orders, and they continued to work
uninterruptedly under the concerned Panchayats from their
respective dates of initial appointment. In the month of August,
2019, the respondent No.1, in exercise of powers conferred under
Section 405 of the Act, 1956, took a policy decision to include the
areas of 18 different Nagar Panchayats/Gram Panchayats into the
territorial limits of the Municipal Corporation, Bilaspur. Pursuant
thereto, a Gazette Notification dated 20.08.2019 was issued,
whereby the said areas surrounding the Municipal Corporation,
Bilaspur, were formally included within its municipal limits.
Sections 405 and 406 of the Act, 1956 provide for the power of
the Governor to include or exclude areas within municipal limits
and stipulate the legal consequences of such inclusion. In terms
of Section 406, upon inclusion of an area within the municipal
limits, the laws relating to Panchayats cease to apply and the
municipal laws come into force, and the State Government is
empowered to issue necessary orders to give effect to such
inclusion and matters incidental or ancillary thereto.  Consequent
upon the issuance of the Gazette Notification dated 20.08.2019,
the respondent No.1 issued instructions dated 28.08.2019 to the
10
Collector, Bilaspur, for management and regulation of works in the
newly included areas and for initiating proceedings for
disestablishment of villages under Section 126(2) of the
Chhattisgarh Panchayat Raj Avam Gram Swaraj Adhiniyam, 1993.
Significantly, Instruction No.7 categorically provided that all
persons working under the concerned Nagar Panchayats/Gram
Panchayats shall be treated as employees of the Municipal
Corporation, and their service conditions shall remain the same as
those prevailing prior to such inclusion. Section 126 of the
Chhattisgarh Panchayat Raj Avam Gram Swaraj Adhiniyam, 1993
deals with disestablishment of villages and empowers the
competent authority to pass consequential orders necessary for
such disestablishment, after following due process. After inclusion
of the concerned Panchayat areas within the Municipal
Corporation, Bilaspur, the lists of employees working under the
respective Panchayats were forwarded to respondent No.2. Upon
receipt of the said lists, respondent No.3 started disbursing the
salaries of the petitioners and other similarly situated employees.
The salaries were paid by the Municipal Corporation, Bilaspur,
continuously up to August 2019. It is the specific case of the
petitioners that, upon such inclusion, their status stood changed
and they were treated as employees of the Municipal Corporation,
Bilaspur. Their salaries were paid by the Municipal Corporation
and they were governed by the service conditions applicable
thereto.  However, to the utter shock and surprise of the
11
petitioners, from July 2020 onwards, their salaries and other
remuneration were abruptly started to be paid through respondent
Nos. 5 to 7, who are independent contractors. It is pertinent to
mention that even after allocating the petitioners under
independent contractors, the Municipal Corporation continued to
issue work orders in favour of the petitioners from time to time and
assigned them municipal duties and responsibilities. The
petitioners submit that they have rendered continuous service for
more than eight years and, therefore, were legitimately entitled to
consideration for regularization. Instead of regularizing their
services, the respondent authorities arbitrarily downgraded their
status by placing them under independent contractors. Aggrieved
thereby, the petitioners submitted several representations before
the competent authorities; however, no action was taken. The
petitioners further submit that due to such allocation under
independent contractors, their status has been reduced from that
of Municipal Corporation employees to contractual workers under
private contractors, thereby seriously affecting their rights of
absorption, service security, and entitlement to remuneration and
other amenities available to municipal employees. The impugned
action of the respondents is arbitrary, illegal, discriminatory, and
contrary to the statutory provisions and settled principles of law,
giving rise to the present writ petition.

4.
Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that the impugned
action of the respondents in allocating the services of the
12
petitioners under independent contractors is wholly arbitrary,
illegal and unsustainable in law. It is contended that the petitioners
have been continuously working under the respondent authorities
for a considerable length of time without any break in service and,
therefore, are legitimately entitled to be granted regular pay scale
commensurate with the nature of duties being performed by them.
Learned counsel further submits that the action of the
respondents is in clear violation and contradiction of the scheme
and mandate of Sections 405 and 406 of the Chhattisgarh
Municipal Corporation Act, 1956, which contemplate continuity of
service and protection of existing service conditions upon
inclusion of Panchayat areas into municipal limits. It is also urged
that payment of salaries to the petitioners through respondent
Nos. 5 to 7, who are independent contractors, is non est in the
eyes of law, without authority and jurisdiction, and amounts to an
impermissible abdication of statutory responsibility by the
Municipal Corporation. Learned counsel emphasizes that the
petitioners fulfill all requisite criteria for grant of regular pay scale,
having rendered long and continuous service, yet they are being
unjustly denied their lawful dues. The impugned action, it is
submitted, is wholly unsustainable and has resulted in grave
mental and financial hardship to the petitioners, warranting
interference by this Court in exercise of its writ jurisdiction.

5.
Learned State counsel, opposing the submissions advanced on
behalf of the petitioners, submits that the petitioners have no
13
vested or legal right to claim regular pay scale or regularization
merely on the basis of long continuance in service. It is contended
that their engagement was purely contractual/temporary in nature
and subject to administrative exigencies. Learned State counsel
further submits that allocation of services through independent
contractors is a policy decision taken in accordance with law and
does not suffer from any arbitrariness or illegality. It is therefore
prayed that the writ petition, being devoid of merit, deserves to be
dismissed.

6.
Learned counsel for the respondent - Municipal Corporation would
submit that the petitioners have filed the present writ petition on
the premise that pursuant to the notification dated 20.08.2019
issued by respondent No.1, whereby 18 Nagar Palikas, Nagar
Panchayats and Gram Panchayats were included within the
territorial limits of the Municipal Corporation, Bilaspur, the
petitioners automatically became employees of the Municipal
Corporation. It is submitted that although, after such inclusion,
salaries of the petitioners were initially disbursed by the Municipal
Corporation for a limited period, the same does not confer upon
them any legal right of permanent absorption or regular
employment under the Corporation.  It is further submitted that, as
is evident from the pleadings themselves, the petitioners were
earlier engaged under different Nagar Panchayats and Gram
Panchayats purely on the basis of requirement and necessity of
work and were never appointed against any sanctioned posts.
14
Their engagement was of daily wage/temporary nature,
commensurate with the needs of the respective Panchayats, and
did not create any vested right in their favour.  Learned counsel
further submits that after inclusion of the areas into the Municipal
Corporation, a specific instruction dated 28.08.2019 (Annexure
P/4) was issued, wherein Clause 7 categorically provides that if
the Municipal Corporation forms an opinion that the services of
any person or officer are not required, it is empowered to
discontinue or decline such services. Therefore, the action of the
respondent Corporation is strictly in accordance with the said
instructions and within the framework of law.  It is also submitted
that all the petitioners are daily wager workers and their names
have been duly enlisted in the placement cell maintained by the
respondent Corporation. The Corporation allocates work to such
workers as and when required, depending upon availability of
work, their capability and utility at different work sites. They are
not regular employees of the Municipal Corporation and are
engaged only as per administrative and operational requirements.
Learned counsel further brings on record that a requisition was
received from an independent contractor, namely M/s Ramesh
Pandey, Bilaspur, for supply of 7 skilled and 18 unskilled
labourers, totaling 25 labourers. Upon such requisition, the
respondent Corporation, vide order dated 05.08.2020, permitted
the said request. Subsequently, a five-member committee was
constituted vide order dated 14.08.2020 to recommend the names
15
of labourers after assessing their capability and suitability. The
petitioners, along with other labourers, were considered by the
said committee and were sent for work purely on the basis of such
assessment.  It is emphatically submitted that the claim of the
petitioners for regularization or grant of regular pay scale cannot
be considered at this stage in view of the settled position of law
governing regularization of daily wage or contractual employees.
The petitioners continue to be part of the placement cell and are
provided work as and when required, and no legal infirmity can be
attributed to the action of the respondent Corporation.  Learned
counsel lastly submits that all other averments made in the writ
petition, save and except those specifically admitted herein, are
denied as false and baseless. In view of the aforesaid facts and
submissions, it is prayed that the writ petition, being devoid of
merit, deserves to be dismissed in the interest of justice and
equity.

7.
I have heard learned counsel for the respective parties and also
perused the documents enclosed along with the petition.

8.
The petitioners have primarily sought directions for regularization
of their services with the Municipal Corporation, Bilaspur, grant of
regular pay scale and consequential benefits, on the ground that
they have rendered long and continuous service and that, upon
inclusion of the concerned Panchayat areas into the Municipal
Corporation, they stood absorbed as municipal employees.  
16

9.
It is not in dispute that the petitioners were initially engaged by
different Gram Panchayats/Nagar Panchayats on temporary/daily
wage basis as per local requirements and were never appointed
against any sanctioned posts following a regular recruitment
process. It is also evident from the record that even after inclusion
of the Panchayat areas into the Municipal Corporation pursuant to
the notification dated 20.08.2019, the petitioners continued to
work as per administrative exigencies and their services were
utilized as and when required.  Merely because salaries of the
petitioners were, for some period, disbursed by the Municipal
Corporation, the same by itself does not create any indefeasible
or vested right in favour of the petitioners for regularization or for
grant of regular pay scale. It is a settled position of law that
regularization cannot be claimed as a matter of right unless the
initial appointment itself was made in accordance with the
constitutional scheme, statutory rules and against sanctioned
posts.  The instructions dated 28.08.2019, relied upon by the
petitioners, cannot be read to confer an automatic right of
absorption or regularization. On the contrary, the said instructions
also empower the Municipal Corporation to assess its requirement
and to discontinue or not to take services of persons who are not
required.

10.
The record further shows that the petitioners are being engaged
through the placement mechanism and their services are being
utilized depending upon availability of work, which cannot be said
17
to be arbitrary or illegal.  In view of the settled legal position
governing regularization of daily wage/temporary employees, and
considering the nature of initial engagement of the petitioners, this
Court does not find any case in favour of the petitioners for
issuance of a writ directing their regularization or grant of regular
pay scale.  However, it is also evident that the petitioners have
been working with the Municipal Corporation for a considerable
period and their services are being utilized for municipal works.
Therefore, while declining the relief of regularization, it is
observed that the Municipal Corporation is at liberty to take the
services of the petitioners and to pass appropriate orders
regarding their further engagement/employment in accordance
with law. It is further observed that if any vacancy arises in future
and a recruitment process is undertaken by the Municipal
Corporation in accordance with law, the Corporation may consider
the previous service rendered by the petitioners and may accord
them appropriate preference, if permissible under the applicable
rules and policy.

11.
Subject to the aforesaid observations, all the writ petitions stand
dismissed.
No order as to costs.
Sd/-

1. This appeal is by the claimant against the award dated 30.09.2016 
passed by the Court of Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Balod, 
District: Balod, (C.G.) in Motor Accident Claim Case No. 29/2016 
wherein, the Tribunal has rejected the claim petition in toto preferred

2. As per claim petition, on 25.01.2016, at about 06:45 am, respondent 
No. 1- Mehtab Khan while driving the offending vehicle Hywa Truck 
bearing registration No. CG04-HT-7265, rashly and negligently, 
dashed the Tractor bearing registration No. CG07-N-4902 attached 
with trolley bearing registration No. CG04-ZG-3202, due to which, the 
said tractor and trolley got damaged. At the time of accident, offending 
vehicle was owned by respondent No. 2 and duly insured with 
respondent No. 3.

3. Due to the said accident, the appellant/claimant, being the owner of 
the trolley, has filed a claim petition under Section 166 of the Motor 
Vehicles Act seeking compensation to the tune of Rs. 70,500/- for the 
damages caused to the trolley. The Tribunal considering the evidence 
led by both the parties dismissed the claim petition filed by the 
claimants on the ground that the damaged caused to the trolley has 
not been proved by the claimant.

4. Learned counsel for the appellant/claimant submits that the offending 
vehicle was involved in the accident which took place with the tractor 
and trolley, due to which, the said tractor-trolley got damaged and the 
same is evident from the statements of AW-2 Krishna Kumar and AW-
3 Rameshwar Yadav, therefore, it is prayed that the damages caused 
3
to the trolley in the said accident shall be compensated to the 
claimant.

5. On the other hand, learned counsel for the respondent No. 2, owner of 
the offending vehicle submits that the claimant has utterly failed to 
prove that the said trolley was actually damaged due to the accident 
and as per the seizure memo of the trolley Ex.P/6, it is not mentioned 
that the said trolley was damaged in the said accident. He further 
submits that the person who has issued the document Ex.P/8, which 
is an estimate, has also not been examined by the appellant and also 
there is no document on record regarding the payment of expenses 
incurred by the appellant, therefore, the learned claims Tribunal has 
rightly dismissed the claim petition.

7. It is not disputed that the incident took place on 25.01.2016 at 06:45 
am, at Paragaon Jhalmala Main Road whereby the respondent No. 1-
Mehtab Khan by driving the offending vehicle in a rash and negligent 
manner, dashed the Tractor bearing registration No. CG07-N-4902 
attached with trolley bearing registration No. CG04-ZG-3202.

8. AW-2 Krishna Kumar/claimant, has stated that on the date of accident, 
the offending vehicle has dashed the tractor from the backside, due to 
which the trolley which was attached with the said tractor was 
damaged and the said trolley was repaired for Rs. 25,500/-. He has 
further stated that he has filed the documents relating to the criminal 
case registered against the driver of the offending vehicle (Exs. P/1 to 
P/9). However, on the contrary, in his cross-examination, he has 
4
admitted that at the time of accident, the said trolley was not insured 
and in Ex.P/6 i.e. Property Seizure Memo, there is no mention that the 
said trolley was damaged. He has also admitted that he has not filed 
any document with regard to mechanical testing of tractor trolley. He 
has also admitted that he has not mentioned the name of a person 
who has issued the document Ex.P/8, which is an estimate and also 
not produced any document with regard to payment of expenses 
incurred by him for repairing of said trolley.

9. AW-3 Rameshwar Yadav, who is the Manager of Durg Tractor 
Showroom, has stated that in the said accident, the trolley was 
damaged and Rs. 25,500/- would be spent for its repairing. He has 
also stated that Ex.P/9 is the estimate receipt. However, on the 
contrary, in cross-examination, this witness has stated that the 
document Ex.P/9 has not been given by him and the description of the 
expenses was also not given by him. He further admitted that in 
Ex.P/8, the expenses relating to trolley was also not been given by 
him and he has also not made any signature in the said document.

10. Thus, from perusal of the statements of AW-2 Krishna Kumar Sahu 
and AW-3 Rameshwar Yadav, it is not proved that in the said 
accident, the said trolley was damaged. This apart, seizure memo 
Ex.P/6, also shows that there was no mention of any damage in the 
said trolley and if the trolley was damaged in the said accident, then it 
would have been specifically mentioned about the condition/damage 
of trolley in the seizure memo as it was mentioned for Tractor. Apart 
from that, the person who has issued the document Ex.P/8, which is 
an estimate, has also not been examined by the appellant to prove the 
5
said fact and that there is no document on record to show that 
claimant has incurred any expenses for repairing of said trolley. In that 
view of the matter, I am of the view that the learned Claims Tribunal, 
after evaluating the evidence available on record, has rightly held that 
the claimant has failed to prove its case. Therefore, the finding 
recorded by the Tribunal is a correct finding based on evidence 
available on record, which needs no interference by this Court.

11.
In view of above, I do not find any infirmity and illegality in the award 
impugned. Accordingly, the appeal being devoid of merit and 
substance is liable to be and is hereby dismissed.

1. The applicant has filed the instant revision under Section 19 of
Chhattisgarh Madhyastham Adhikaran, 1983 being aggrieved with
the impugned order dated 07.12.2022 (Annexure A/1) passed by
Chhattisgarh Madhyastham Adhikaran, Raipur in Reference Case
No. 03/2021 whereby the Tribunal dismissed the reference petition
moved by the applicant.

2. Brief facts of the case as projected by the applicant, are that the
2
applicant moved an application under section 7 of Chhattisgarh
Madhyastham Adhikaran Adhiniyam, 1983 against the present
respondents for recovery of Rs 1,27,70,859/- (One Crore Twenty
Seven lakhs Seventy Thousand Eight Hundred and Fifty-nine
Only) from the respondents. The applicant is a partnership firm &
a registered B class contractors with various departments of the
state of Chhattisgarh being represented herein through partner
namely Anand Kumar Soni. The contract was awarded to the
applicant through letter dated 05.06.2017 and subsequently work
order was issued to the applicant for construction of 200 seat Boys
Hostel at Jora, Raipur for the sum of Rs. 305.33 Lakh. After
issuance of work order, the applicant started the construction on
the project, after which the present respondents changed the
place of construction from Jora to Dunda. Thereafter, the applicant
requested respondent no.2 to revise the rates for another proposal
of construction. The respondent authorities assured the applicant
that the revised proposal for construction work would be finalized
and the applicant was pressurized to continue & complete the
work.

3. As per directions of the respondents, applicant started work in
changed place as per design & guideline according to the
Assistant/Sub Engineer. Respondent authorities, without any
information stopped the payment to the applicant. Thereafter, the
applicant sent reminder letters dated 07.11.2017, 15.12.2017.
26.12.2017, 10.01.2018, 27.02.2018, 02.04.2018, 05.04.2018,
09.04.2018, 13.06.2018, 29.06.2018 & 14.01.2019 to the
respondent authorities for making the payments. Respondent
authorities did not respond the reminder letters sent by the
applicant. The respondent authorities did not make payment since
28.03.2018 and due to delay on the part of the respondent
authorities in making the payment, the cost of work is rising day by
day. The respondent authorities neither released the payments
over the pending bills nor rejected any claims of the applicant due
to which, the applicant is facing huge financial loss and financial
3
hardships.

4. As the respondent authorities did not reply the applicant’s letters,
the applicant was left with no option but to invoke the Clause 28 of
the contract.  As per the Clause 28 of the conditions of the
contract, if any dispute arises the same has to be referred to the
Superintendent Engineer, but since there is no post of the
Superintendent Engineer in the department of Tribal welfare due
to which, the applicant sent a legal notice dated 17/11/2020 to
respondents No.2 & 3 for seeking clarification about the post of
Superintendent Engineer. Copy of Legal Notice dated 17/11/2020
along with receipt dated 18.11.2020 are collectively annexed
herewith as Annexure-A/2 (colly). The respondent authorities did
not respond to the legal notice dated 17.11.2020 sent by the
applicant. Thereafter, the applicant filed a reference petition before
the Chhattisgarh Madhyastham Adhikaran, Raipur, wherein the
respondent authorities appeared and filed the preliminary
objection on 04.01.2022 for dismissal of reference petition as the
petition is not maintainable because the applicant did not refer the
dispute to the competent authority as per Clause 28 of the
contract. Copy of the reference petition is annexed as Annexure-
A/3.

5. After hearing counsel for the parties and after perusal of the
records, the Chhattisgarh Madhyastham Adhikaran, Raipur,
passed the impugned order dated 07.12.2022 (Annexure A/1)
rejecting the reference petition of the applicant on the ground of
maintainability. Hence, the instant revision has been filed by the
applicant.

6. Learned counsel for the applicant submits that the impugned order
dated 07.12.2022 (Annexure A/1) is contrary to law, facts and
circumstances of the case. The learned Tribunal ought to have
appreciated the fact that the applicant tried to invoke the Clause-
28 of the contract by referring the dispute to the Superintendent
Engineer, but since there is no post of the Superintendent
4
Engineer in the department of Tribal welfare due to which the
applicant sent a legal notice dated 17/11/2020 to respondents
No.02 & 03 for seeking clarification about the post of
Superintendent Engineer. But since the respondent authorities did
not respond to the legal notice dated 17.11.2020, the applicant
was left with no option but to file the reference petition before the
Chhattisgarh Madhyastham Adhikaran. The learned Tribunal ought
to have perused the documents attached along with the reference
petition and also ought to have appreciated the fact that the
applicant approached the respondent authorities for clearance of
the pending bills, but in spite of clearing the pending bills, the
respondent authorities arbitrarily stopped the payments to the
applicant.

7. The learned Tribunal erroneously held that, it is ample clear in the
contract itself that the word “Superintending Engineer” used in
Clause-28 of the contract means the Superintending Engineer of
P.W.D. Circle (Civil) within whose jurisdiction the Village Dunda is
situated. The learned Tribunal without appreciating  the facts and
circumstances of the case and the conditions of the agreement,
passed impugned order which is liable to be dismissed.  However,
it is further submitted by learned counsel for the applicant that this
is a bonafide mistake on the part of the applicant to interpret the
section of contract, therefore, liberty may be granted to him to file
fresh representation before the competent authority as per Clause
28 of the contract.

8. Learned counsel for the respondents/State strongly opposes the
prayer of the applicant and submits that it is clear from the
contents of the contract that the term “Superintending Engineer”
means the Superintending Engineer of the concerned P.W.D.
Circle (Civil and Electrical) as the case may be. Therefore,  the
reference petition filed by the applicant was on false and frivolous
grounds and the learned Tribunal passed impugned order in
accordance with law and as per conditions of the contract.
Therefore, this revision petition being without any substance is
5
liable to be and is hereby dismissed.

11. In Condition of Contract the term Superintending Engineer,
Chief Engineer and Executive Engineer have been defined.
Definition clause 2 provides the meaning of expressions used in
the contract. As per definition clause 2 :- 
2(g)- The term "Superintending Engineer" means the
Superintending Engineer of the concerned P.W.D. Circle (Civil
and Electrical) as the case may be. 
(h)- The term "Executive Engineer"/ "Engineer-in- Charge" /
"Divisional Officer" means the Executive Engineer of the
concerned P.W.D. Division.
11.Learned Tribunal after observing provisions of Madhyastham
Adhikaran Adhiniyam, 1983 and the conditions of contract, passed
the impugned order which is in accordance with law. This Court
finds no illegality or perversity in the order impugned and,
therefore, this Court is not inclined to interfere in the impugned
order.
12.Looking to the facts and circumstances of the case, this revision
petition being without any substance is liable to be and is hereby
dismissed. However, the applicant shall be at liberty to file fresh
representation within one month before the competent authority to
decide the same as per the conditions of contract after hearing the
parties within four months from the date of receiving the
representation of the applicant.

10. The Sub-Divisional Officer(R), Korba has passed the order on 
14.02.2024 stating that the claim site is part of the protected forest 
area number P-989. A survey error occurred, and it has not been 
proven that the land undisputedly belongs to the petitioner. The 
fundamental proof of ownership is lawful possession of the land, 
which the petitioner has not been able to prove. The claim site is 
located entirely within the undisputed protected forest area 
compartment number Old 2200 P, New 989 P. In the 2005-06 
Revenue Survey, this disputed land was recorded as Khasra No. 
374, a large shrub forest. The Forest Department's unauthorized 
occupation of the petitioner’s land is not proven.

11. On perusal of the order dated 27.01.2014 (Annexure P-4) passed 
by the Collector- Korba/respondent No.6, it reveals that as per 
punchnama report, 2013, the subject land belonged to the 
petitioner. The name of the petitioner and her ancestors was 
registered in the records, rights records/Mashati Khasra/B-1, then 
why is it not registered at present? Further, it reveals that the trial 
Court also sought an investigation report from the Forest 
Department, Korba, and the Land Records, Korba, regarding the 
petitioner’s land. Following this, the Forest Department and the 
Land Records jointly inspected the site and prepared a panchnama 
on 26.02.2013, which stated that the subject land belonged to the 
petitioner. However, the Forest Department stated that the 
petitioner’s land was surrounded by barbed wire by the Forest 
8
Department.

12. Further, it is undisputed fact that the petitioner belongs to Pahadi 
Korwa tribe which has been identified and categorized by the 
Government of India as a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group 
(PVTG). The President of India, under Article 342 of the 
Constitution, makes public announcements to declare which tribes 
or tribal communities are to be considered "Scheduled Tribes" 
(STs). Within this broader category, the more vulnerable groups 
are sub-categorized as PVTGs for targeted development. The 
Korwa tribe are often referred to as the "adopted children of the 
President of India" due to this special, more vulnerable status, 
which implies a greater need for focused Government attention 
and development.

13. Looking to the above facts, it is directed to the respondent 
authorities that if the name of the petitioner and her ancestors was 
registered in the revenue records in the year 2013, then why is it 
not registered at present? The Respondent Authorities are directed 
to minutely inspect the revenue records with regard to subject land 
and whose name entered in the records since long and thereafter 
pass appropriate orders as early as possible. It is further directed 
that during the course of inspection, if it is found that the subject 
land is in the name of the petitioner and her ancestors, the 
respondent authorities are directed to initiate the proceedings for 
9
grant of compensation in favour of the petitioner as per the extant 
policy/statute.

14. With the aforesaid observations and directions, the instant petition 
stands disposed of.

1.
By way of this writ appeal filed under Section 2 (1) of the 
Chhattisgarh High Court (Appeal to Division Bench Act, 2006), appellant 
has sought for the following relief:-
“It is, therefore, prayed that the Hon'ble Court may be kind 
enough to allow the Writ Appeal in the interest of justice by 
quashing the impugned order and may be kind enough to 
2
pass appropriate order in the interest of justice.”

2.
The present writ appeal has been preferred by the appellant - 
workman challenging the order dated 16.01.2019 passed by learned Single 
Judge in WPL No. 144 of 2014, whereby writ petition filed by respondents 
No. 1 to 3 / Employer was allowed in part and Rs.3,00,000/- as a lump sum 
monetary compensation was awarded to the appellant/  workman in lieu of 
his reinstatement in service as full and final settlement of the award. 
Aforesaid writ petition i.e.  WPL No. 144 of 2014 had been filed against 
order dated 01.05.2014 passed by Labour Court No. 1, Raipur 
(Chhattisgarh) in Case No. 117/I.D. Act/2000 /Reference whereby learned 
Labour Court has granted relief to the appellant herein for his reinstatement 
in employment  without backwages.

3.
The brief facts relevant for adjudication of the present case are that 
the appellant / workman was engaged by the respondents / State as a daily 
wage employee against the vacant post of Gauze Reader on 05.08.1989. 
The said employment continued up till 30.01.2000, and from 31.01.2000 
onwards, the services of the appellant/workman was retrenched by the 
respondents/State by paying salary of one month in lieu of notice and after 
about few days retrenchment compensation was also paid to him.

4.
The appellant/workman initially raised an industrial dispute against 
discontinuance of his employment under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 
(henceforth “ID Act”) before the Appropriate Government and the 
Appropriate Government, in turn, made a reference to the Labour Court, 
Raipur for adjudication of the following terms of reference :-  
3
“Whether the termination of service of the worker by the 
State was legal and justified, and if not to what relief he 
is entitled for.”

5.
Learned Labour Court No. 1, Raipur, Chhattisgarh registered the 
case as Case No. 117/I.D. Act/2000 /Reference and after affording due 
opportunity of hearing & by appreciating oral and documentary evidence 
adduced by the parties, vide order dated 01.05.2014 granted relief to the 
appellant / workman holding that his retrenchment from service was bad in 
law and illegal and further ordered of his reinstatement in service without 
backwages, which was challenged by appellant- workman by filing writ 
petition, as has been mentioned in preceding paragraph of this order.

6.
Learned Single Judge, after appreciating oral & documentary 
evidence available on record, vide its impugned order dated 16.01.2019, 
writ petition filed by respondents No. 1 to 3/ Employer was partly allowed 
and Rs.3,00,000/- as lump sum monetary compensation was awarded to 
the appellant/workman in lieu of his reinstatement in service as full & final 
settlement of the award.

7.
Learned counsel appearing for the appellant / workman would submit 
that learned Single Judge itself has held that in exercising of power of writ 
jurisdiction, High Court has limited scope to interfere with the award passed 
by the Labour Court and, therefore, it should  not venture on the finding of 
the court below, despite that learned Single Judge has ventured beyond 
the scope.  It is further submitted that learned Labour Court has held that 
retrenchment of appellant was not valid retrenchment and the same has 
4
been done without adhering the provisions of Section 25 of the ID Act, 
therefore, order passed by Labour Court ought not to have been interfered 
with. Further provision of Sections 25-G and 25-H of ID Act, which 
envisage principle of “last come first go”, has not been complied with by 
respondent authorities and learned Single Judge is absolutely unjustified in 
overreaching the binding precedent of the Apex Court in alike matters. 
7.1    Learned counsel for the appellant / workman further submits that 
learned Single Judge has erred in granting lump-sum compensation to the 
appellant / workman in lieu of his reinstatement in service, though he has 
completed more than 11 years of his services under the respondent No. 3 
on the date of his retrenchment from service i.e. 31.01.2000.  He would 
further submit that since the stay was granted by the Single Bench of this

order passed by the Labour Court, the appellant was not reinstated in 
service, but instead thereof, he is being paid last pay drawn in compliance 
of provisions contained in Section 17-B of the ID Act, which is equivalent to 
the work, therefore, he be treated that he is continuous in his employment. 
Referring to judgment rendered by Division Bench of this Court in the 
matter of Tukaram vs. State of Chhattisgarh & others and other 
connected matters1, he would submit that in the aforesaid case, it has 
been held that, after the order of Industrial Court quashing the termination 
order would mean that no order of termination was ever existed and the 
services of the workman is in continuation, as order of his reinstatement 
was stayed by this Court  but paying last pay drawn by respondents to the

WPS No. 1703 of 2015 & other connecte matters, decided on 16.05.2017
5
appellant in compliance of Section 17-B of the ID Act, amounts to, that

the appellant would be 30 years under the respondents No. 3 & 4, 
therefore, the appellant /workman not only deserves to be reinstated in his

therefore, findings of the learned Single Judge on every counts are illegal,

prayer made by appellant / workman, learned Single Judge has no 
jurisdiction to mould the relief granted by the Labour Court, but by wrongly 
applying the law laid down by the Apex Court in the cases of Bharat 
Sanchar Nigam Limited v. Bhurumal
 
 2 and District Development 
Officer & Anr. v. Satish Kantilal Amrelia
 
 3 has moulded the relief granted 
by the Labour Court.
2
2014 (7) SCC 177
3
(2018) 12 SCC 298
6

8.
To substantiate his submissions, learned counsel for the appellant / 
workman placed reliance upon the judgment of the Division Bench of this 
Court in the matter of Tukaram (supra) and also upon the judgment of the 
Supreme Court in the matter of State of Chhattisgarh & another v. 
Karishna Kumar Kashyap

4.  Learned counsel has also referred various 
judgments in memo of appeal in support of his submission.

9.
Learned counsel appearing for the respondents / State submits that 
the order passed by the learned Single Judge is a well reasoned & merited 
order, with no ambiguity or perversity whatsoever and therefore the writ 
appeal deserves to be rejected. He submits that, since the stay was 
granted by the learned Single Judge on 22.09.2014 against  the 
appellant/workman, therefore, in compliance of the order passed by the 
Labour Court, the appellant was not reinstated in service, but instead 
thereof, he is being paid last pay drawn in compliance of provisions 
contained in Section 17-B of the ID Act, but the argument made on behalf 
of the appellant/employee cannot be appreciated that since in compliance 
of Section 17-B of the Industrial Dispute Act, he is being paid last pay 
drawn, therefore, it is presumed that he is continuously of his employment, 
because last pay drawn is being given in compliance of statutory provisions 
contained in Section 17-B of the ID Act, which cannot be equated with the 
continuance of work.  He would further submit the law laid down by the 
Division Bench of this Court in the matter of Tukaram vs. State of 
Chhattisgarh & other connected matters (supra), relied upon by counsel 
for the appellant, would not be applicable in the present case for the reason 
4
Special Leave Petition (C) No. 36862/2016, decided on 1st May, 2017. 
7
that issue which was raised in the case of Tukaram (supra) is with respect 
to counting of period from the initial date of appointment till the 
reinstatement was made and subsequent period as continuous service for 
the purpose of calculating the length of service whereas the same is not 
the issue in the instant case because after the award passed by Labour 
Court, an interim order was passed by the learned Single Judge whereby in 
compliance of provision contained in Section 17-B of the Industrial 
Disputes Act, the appellant is being paid last pay drawn and the appellant 
is out of service since 2000 and has not worked on the regular sanctioned 
post since 2000, hence, on facts, the present case is distinguishable from 
the fact of the case mentioned in  Tukaram (supra).  So far as judgment 
relied on by the appellant passed by Hon’ble Supreme Court in the matter 
of State of Chhattisgarh and another v. Karishna Kumar Kashyap 
(supra) is also not applicable to the present case and distinguishable on 
facts because that was the case where workman was working after the 
award passed by the Labour Court whereas in the present case, after order 
of retrenchment, the workman has not worked since January, 2000. 
Therefore, appeal is liable to be dismissed.

10.
We have heard learned counsel appearing for the parties and 
perused the material available on record with utmost circumspection.

11.
Perusal of impugned order would go to show that learned Single 
Judge after going through the record has held in paragraph 17 as under :-
“17.
This Court therefore has no hesitation in reaching 
to the conclusion that so far as the finding of the Labour 
Court holding the termination to be bad in law on 
8
account of non-compliance of mandatory provisions of 
Section 25 of the Industrial Disputes Act does not 
warrant interference and the same stands affirmed.

12.
Aforesaid finding recorded by the learned Single Judge has not been 
challenged by the respondents /State, therefore, the said finding recorded 
by learned Single Judge has attained finality, that, termination of 
appellant/workman from service by respondents authorities was bad in law, 
as the same has been made without complying the mandatory provisions 
of Section 25 of the ID Act, therefore, various grounds raised in the writ 
petitions to show that  retrenchment of appellant / workman was against 
the law need not wants further consideration by this Court.

13.
Undisputedly, it is found that retrenchment of the appellant is bad in 
law, but whether his reinstatement, can be made, has been considered by 
learned Single Judge in paragraph 18 as under :- 
“21.  Given the aforesaid factual matrix of the case what 
requires consideration at this juncture is whether it would 
be advisable, fruitful and practical directing the State 
Government to now after a period of more than 19 years 
take the employee back in service. True it is that the 
Hon’ble Supreme Court in the past has been holding that 
once when the termination is held to be bad in law, the 
automatic consequence of that is the entitlement of 
reinstatement with all consequential benefits. But of late, 
the Hon’ble Supreme Court has been of the view that the 
granting of reinstatement should be only after taking into 
9
consideration the entire factual matrix of the case and in a 
given factual scenario, if the Court finds the reinstatement 
part to be not very advisable, it can mold the relief to the 
extent of granting compensation in lieu of 
reinstatement.........”

14.
Learned Single Judge, while considering the law laid down by the 
Apex Court in case of Satish Kantilal Amerelia
 
  (supra),  Hari Nandan 
Prasad & Anr. v. Employer I/R to Management of Food Corporation 
of India & Anr.5 and Bhuvnesh Kumar Dwivedi v. Hindalco Industries 
Limited
 
 6 has held in paragraph 21 to 23, which are reproduced as under :- 
“21. Coming to the various judgments which have been 
relied upon by the counsel for the worker, if we go through 
the contents of these judgments, there is no quarrel so far 
as the ratio or the principles that have been laid down in 
all these judgments and which still hold good. However 
what cannot be brushed aside is the fact that there has 
been a slight shift from the earlier position that was taken 
by the Hon’ble Supreme Court and that is the power 
which has now been given to the Labour Courts and even 
to the High Courts to see whether it would be equitable at 
this juncture to order for a reinstatement in service in the 
factual backdrop of each case. Particularly, the 
judgments, which have been laid down by the Hon’ble 
Supreme Court after the decision rendered by it in 
5
2014 (7) SCC 190
6
2014 (11) SCC 85
10
“Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited v. Bhurumal” 2014(7) 
SCC 177 and which has further been reiterated time and 
again, which recently now stands also reiterated in the 
case of “Satish Kantilal Amrelia” (supra).

22.
Under the aforesaid factual matrix of the present 
case and also taking note of the judgments discussed in 
the preceding paragraphs, this Court is of the opinion that 
since as enumerated earlier, the worker has in fact 
physically worked with the department only for a period of 
about 3 years between 1990 to January, 2000 and from 
February, 2000 till date i.e. 2018 he has not physically 
worked with the department, as he has been paid the last 
wage drawn without reinstatement even after the award of 
the Labour Court till date. However for the reasons, which 
emerged from the discussions made in the preceding 
paragraphs and the fact that the worker is out of 
employment for a period of now over 19 years, it is a fit 
case where the order of reinstatement would not be 
equitable or justified at this point of time and this Court 
also does not have any hesitation in holding that in the 
given facts it would not fall under any of those exceptional 
circumstances entailing reinstatement considering it to be 
an exceptional circumstances, which were envisaged by 
the Hon’ble Supreme Court while deciding in the case of 
“Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited” (supra).
11

23.    Thus, this Court finds that it is a fit case, where the 
worker could be awarded compensation in lieu of 
reinstatement as full and final settlement of his claim, 
keeping in line with the ratio laid down by the Hon’ble 
Supreme Court in its judgment starting from “Bharat 
Sanchar Nigam Limited” (supra) and which stood 
reiterated right up till the judgment in the case of “Satish 
Kantilal Amrelia” (supra). This Court considering the 
entire facts and circumstances of the case orders that the 
worker would be entitled for an amount of Rs.3 lacs as a 
lump sum monetary compensation in lieu of 
reinstatement in service as full and final settlement of 
award.”

15.
Contention of learned counsel appearing for the appellant /workman 
is that order of reinstatement of appellant / workman passed by learned 
Labour Court was stayed by the learned Single Bench of this Court, vide 
order dated 22.09.2014, therefore, appellant was not re-instated in service, 
instead thereof, he is being paid last pay drawn in compliance of provision 
contained in Section 17-B of the I.D. Act, therefore, appellant be treated as 
continuation in his employment, in such situation, learned Single Judge has 
wrongly appreciated the fact that appellant was out of employment for 
almost 19 years.  It was also contention of learned counsel for the appellant 
that appellant has not sought for any relief of lump-sum compensation, 
rather he has prayed for regularization in service, despite that learned 
Single Judge has moulded the relief granted by the Labour Court, which is 
12
against the law.

16.
Aforesaid contention has been very well dealt by learned Single 
Judge in its impugned judgment, relying upon the law laid down by Hon'ble 
Supreme Court, as has been mentioned in preceding paragraphs of the 
judgment. Therefore, we have no hesitation to uphold the observations 
made by learned Single Judge in concluding paragraph 21 to 23 of the 
impugned judgment.

17.
It is apt to note here that in earlier decisions of Apex Court, the view 
had been taken that if the termination of an employee was found to be 
illegal, the relief of reinstatement would ordinarily follow, but subsequently 
view of Apex Court was shifted from aforesaid legal position and at present 
in catena of judgments, Hon'ble Supreme Court has consistently held that 
relief by way of re-instatement with backwages will not be automatic and 
may be absolutely inappropriate in fact situation of the case, even though 
the termination of an employee is found to be in contravention of the 
prescribed procedure under the law and in such a situation compensation 
instead of reinstatement has been held to meet the ends of justice.

18.
Learned Single Judge while referring various judgments has rightly 
held that in recent past slightly shift from the earlier legal position has been 
taken by the Supreme Court. Judgment referred to /relied upon by the 
appellant were prior to aforesaid shifting of the view by the Apex Court.  In 
this regard, we think it appropriate to quote here observations made by 
Apex Court in the matter of Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited (supra) in 
paragraphs 33 to 35, which read as under :- 
13
“33. It is clear from the reading of the aforesaid 
judgments that the ordinary principle of grant of 
reinstatement with full back wages, when the 
termination is found to be illegal is not applied 
mechanically in all cases. While that may be a position 
where services of a regular/permanent workman are 
terminated illegally and/or mala fide and/or by way of 
victimisation, unfair labour practice, etc. However, 
when it comes to the case of termination of a daily-
wage worker and where the termination is found illegal 
because of a procedural defect, namely, in violation of 
Section 25-F of the Industrial Disputes Act, this Court 
is consistent in taking the view that in such cases 
reinstatement with back wages is not automatic and 
instead the workman should be given monetary 
compensation which will meet the ends of justice. 
Rationale for shifting in this direction is obvious.

34. The reasons for denying the relief of reinstatement 
in such cases are obvious. It is trite law that when the 
termination is found to be illegal because of non-
payment of retrenchment compensation and notice 
pay as mandatorily required under Section 25-F of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, even after reinstatement, it is 
always open to the management to terminate the 
services of that employee by paying him the 
retrenchment compensation. Since such a workman 
was working on daily-wage basis and even after he is 
reinstated, he has no right to seek regularisation [see 
State of Karnataka v. Umadevi (3)17]. Thus when he 
cannot claim regularisation and he has no right to 
continue even as a daily-wage worker, no useful 
purpose is going to be served in reinstating such a 
workman and he can be given monetary 
14
compensation by the Court itself inasmuch as if he is 
terminated again after reinstatement, he would receive 
monetary compensation only in the form of 
retrenchment compensation and notice pay. In such a 
situation, giving the relief of reinstatement, that too 
after a long gap, would not serve any purpose.

35. We would, however, like to add a caveat here. 
There may be cases where termination of a daily-
wage worker is found to be illegal on the ground that 
it was resorted to as unfair labour practice or in 
violation of the principle of last come first go viz. 
while retrenching such a worker daily wage juniors to 
him were retained. There may also be a situation that 
persons junior to him were regularised under some 
policy but the workman concerned terminated. In 
such circumstances, the terminated worker should 
not be denied reinstatement unless there are some 
other weighty reasons for adopting the course of 
grant of compensation instead of reinstatement. In 
such cases, reinstatement should be the rule and 
only in exceptional cases for the reasons stated to be 
in writing, such a relief can be denied.”

19.
Aforesaid view was further reiterated by the Apex Court in the matter 
of Satish Kantilal Amrelia (Supra), Hari Nandan Prasad and Anr. 
(supra), Bhuvnesh Kumar Dwivedi (supra) and State of Uttrakhand & 
another Vs. Rajkumar7.

20.
Thus, similar issue, involved in the instant case has been considered 
by the Apex Court in afore-cited judgments that, if employment of dailywage 
workman has been terminated illegally because of procedural defect of the 
7
(2019) 14 SCC 353
15
ID Act, Hon'ble Apex Court is consistent in taking a view that in such cases, 
reinstatement would not automatic and instead the workman should be 
given monetary compensation, which will meet the ends of justice. 
Rationale for shifting in this direction has been considered by the Apex 
Court holding that even after reinstatement, it is always open to the 
management to terminate the services of that employee by paying him the 
retrenchment compensation and following other procedures. Since such a 
workman was working on daily-wage basis and even after he is reinstated, 
he has no right to seek regularisation and when he cannot claim 
regularization and he has no right to continue even as a daily-wage worker, 
no useful purpose would be served in reinstating such a workman and he 
can be given monetary compensation by the Court.

21.
Applying the ratio of law laid down by the Apex Court in the afore-
cited cases in the facts of the present case, we do not find any ground 
showing that employment of appellant has been terminated by respondents 
/ State by playing unfair labour practice or any exceptional circumstances, 
as has been considered by the Apex Court in case of Bharat Sanchar 
Nigam Limited (supra).

22.
Although, appellant is being paid last pay drawn, but it is being made 
in a statutory compliance of Section 17-B of the ID Act, 1947, which cannot 
be equated with the actual working with the respondents- Department. Only 
on this count, appellant cannot be granted relief of re-instatement in 
service, particularly, considering the consistent view taken by the Apex 
Court from last several years. 
16

23.
In view of the foregoing discussion, we are of the considered view 
that learned Single Judge has not committed any error in granting monetary 
compensation in lieu of re-instatement of appellant/workman in service but 
appellant had worked with respondents Department from 05.08.1989 to 
31.01.2000, thereafter, he was retrenched from service.  Hence, 
considering his such long period of service we think it just & proper that 
monetary compensation be enhanced from Rs.3,00,000/- to Rs. 5,00,000/-. 
Therefore, we direct respondents to pay monetary compensation to the 
appellant to the tune of Rs. 5,00,000/- in lieu of reinstatement of appellant 
workman in service with full & final settlement of the award.

24.
Let amount of Rs.5,00,000/- be paid by respondent/State to the 
appellant / workman within a period of three months from the date of 
receipt / production of copy of this order.  If aforesaid amount is not paid 
within stipulated period, then respondents shall be liable to pay interest 
@ 9% per annum on the said amount.

25.
In view of the foregoing, the writ appeal is partly allowed to the extent 
indicated hereinabove. No order as to costs.

1. The petitioner was appointed on a contract basis as 
Radiographer in the Community Health Centre, Patthalgaon 
District-Jashpur on 14.07.2003. The contract service was 
approved on 31.03.2018, however, before completion of the said 
2
period he was removed from his contract vide order dated 
18.09.2017 (Annexure P-1), as the regular Radiographer has 
been posted in place of the petitioner.

2. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that the contract 
appointment was for the period of 31.03.2018, however, it has 
been stated that this order of contract appointment will be 
terminated, if the post will be fulfilled by the regular posting  or 
by way of promotion. However, some other Radiographer has 
been appointed, which is not a regular posting, as such the 
impugned order is not accordance with law. It was verbally also 
prayed that if the posts are lying vacant, the petitioner may be 
given contract appointment and he may be given salary to the 
remaining part of service.

3. On the other hand, learned counsel for the respondent  stated 
that since the petitioner was appointed as on a contract basis 
and in the order itself it has been stated that after 
recruitment/posting of any regular employee his services will be 
terminated, as such there is no illegality in the order so far as 
the  verbal prayer has been made by the learned counsel for the 
petitioner stating that since the period of contract was upto 
31.03.2018, it was not expired, therefore, the petitioner may be 
granted the salary up to the said period cannot be accepted.

4. I have heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the 
material available on record as well as the appointment order.

5. From the appointment order itself it is apparent that it was a 
contract service in which it has been specifically mentioned that 
3
it can be terminated as and when regular Radiographer is 
posted since during the contract service of the petitioner the 
regular Radiographer has been posted, as such the services of 
the petitioner has been terminated and therefore, there is no 
illegality in passing of the impugned order. So far as, the claim 
of the petitioner in respect of grant of salary from the 
termination order dated 18.09.2017 upto 31.03.2018 is 
concerned, it can not be granted for two reasons firstly the 
petitioner has not prayed about the same in the writ petition 
further in the appointment order itself it is stated that the 
service of the petitioner is till the contract period or on regular 
appointment of Radiographer, as such even after the petitioner 
has been terminated before the period of contract period, 
looking to the aforesaid fact he can not be given the salary/back 
wages as prayed orally by the petitioner.

6. In view of the aforesaid aspect of the matter the petition being 
sense of merit is hereby dismissed.

7. Accordingly, instant petition is dismissed.

3 / 8
that possession of the suit house be also provided after execution of sale 
deed.

3.
Defendant submitted written statement to the pleadings made by 
plaintiff and had denied all adverse pleadings made therein. It was pleaded 
that in the house situated at Village- Lendhra (Chhote), defendant No.1 
resides along with his other brothers separately. He had denied of obtaining 
hand loan of Rs.2,21,000/- from plaintiff and has also denied the alleged 
commitment of returning amount after three months. Agreement is stated to 
be forged and fabricated.

4.
Learned trial Court based on pleadings made by respective parties had 
formulated as many as five issues for consideration and after conclusion of 
trial had allowed the suit in part granting decree of refund of money of 
Rs.2,21,000/- in favour of plaintiff with interest at the rate of 6%.

5.
Learned counsel for appellant/defendant No.1 would submit that 
learned trial Court even after recording a finding that no contract has ever 
been effectuated in between plaintiff and defendant No.1 and therefore no 
relief in terms of performance of contract can be granted to plaintiff, grant of 
decree in favour of plaintiff is erroneous. He also contended that when 
execution of document is denied, it is for the plaintiff to prove signature of 
defendant on the document based on the opinion of handwriting expert . In 
absence of any such opinion, genuineness of Ex. P-1 is highly suspicious. 
Pleading and evidence brought in record by plaintiff did not satisfy the 
manner and proof of mortgage nor the title deed of mortgaged property. 
Learned trial Court erred in coming to conclusion that plaintiff proved the valid 
4 / 8
execution of Ex.P-1. As such, finding recorded pursuant to issues No. 1 to 3 
with regard to valid execution of document Ex.P-1 was illegal and perverse.

6.
Learned counsel for respondent No.1/plaintiff opposed submission of 
learned counsel for the appellant/defendant and would submit that even if the 
heading is with regard to “specific performance of contract”, however, in the 
plaint, there is specific prayer made by the plaintiff of refund of amount of 
Rs.2,21,000/- from defendant and, therefore, learned trial Court justified in 
passing the impugned judgment which does not call for any interference.

7.
I have heard learned counsel for the parties and also perused the 
record of learned trial Court.

8.
So as to appreciate submission of learned counsel for appellant/ 
defendant No.1, I have perused the plaint filed by respondent No.1/plaintiff, 
perusal of which, would show that under heading of suit it is mentioned as 
"suit for specific performance of contract" value of suit as Rs.2,21,000/-. In 
the body of plaint, it is mentioned that defendant No.1 obtained loan from 
plaintiff with an assurance to return back the same within short time and an 
agreement in that regard was executed on 21.07.2014. Agreement is filed as 
Ex.P-1. Perusal of agreement would show that it relates to house situated at 
Deeh. It further mentions that against house situated at village- Lendhra, 
defendant No.1 obtained the amount of Rs.2,21,000/-. There is further 
pleading made in the agreement that the amount is to be returned within 3 
months and if defendant tries to delay in making payment or avoid the same, 
plaintiff would be at liberty to file appropriate proceedings/suit in Court of 
competent jurisdiction, to get sale deed registered in his favour by order of 
5 / 8
the Court. Agreement is filed as Ex.P-1. Legal notice sent by plaintiff is filed 
as Ex.P-2. Plaintiff himself is examined as PW1 to prove the pleadings made 
in the plaint and one Bansi Sahu as PW2. Plaintiff in his examination- in-chief 
has stated about hand loan taken by defendant of Rs.2,21,000/-. Agreement 
entered into between the plaintiff  and defendant No.1 was also written down 
in stamp paper. In cross-examination, this witness stood firm with the 
pleading with regard to advancing of loan to defendant No.1. This witness 
was cross-examined, however, nothing adverse has come in his evidence. 
He also stated that defendant is resident of same village and community as of 
plaintiff. He also called for panchayat which was convened after about one 
month from the date of request made by him. Bansi Sahu (PW2) also 
supported the case of plaintiff. He further stated that the village of which he is 
resident of is a small village and, therefore, almost all persons know each 
other.

9.
Defendant No.1/appellant is examined as DW1. However, he denied all 
the evidence which was brought, but for execution of agreement Ex.P-1. He 
admits that his photograph is pasted on agreement, however, he denied his 
signature. In para-9 of his cross-examination, he admitted that though he 
stated that agreement is forged and fabricated, however, he has not made 
any report/complaint to concerned police station in this regard nor any 
proceedings is initiated against plaintiff but denied the mortgaging of house. 
Kushal  Sahu is examined as DW2 . In his cross-examination, he admitted 
that defendant along with his brother is residing jointly in the said house 
which was the ancestral house in which defendant is also having his share. 
6 / 8
From the evidence of this witness, it is appearing that he is not the witness to 
document Ex.P-1.

10.
From aforementioned evidence available in record, it is appearing that 
plaintiff proved that defendant No.1 had taken hand loan from plaintiff. 
Document Ex.P-1 is also executed, however, he refused to return back the 
money mentioned therein.

11.
So far as the main ground raised by learned counsel for 
appellant/defendant that from contents of document Ex.P-1 it does not 
appear that it is an agreement to sell and therefore direction of the Court to 
refund the amount to plaintiff of Rs.2,21,000/- is bad in law is concerned, true 
it is, in heading of plaint there is mention of "suit for specific performance of 
contract" however in relief clause there is specific prayer for recovery of 
amount of Rs.2,21,000/-. Grant of decree of specific performance is  prayed 
in alternate, which is even otherwise a discretionary jurisdiction of the Court, 
the Court may either grant the decree for specific performance of contract 
and if there is further prayer of refund of money, learned trial Court may 
consider the second/ alternate relief of refund of amount and therefore in the 
opinion of this Court, judgment and decree passed by learned trial Court of 
refund the amount of agreement Ex.P-1 cannot be said to be without 
jurisdiction. Merely giving heading of suit will not be a decisive factor but the 
entire pleadings and relief sought is also to be looked into for considering the 
grant of relief to plaintiff in his suit.

12.
The nature of document said to be executed between the parties and 
intention of the parties at the time of execution of document has to be culled 
7 / 8
out from the recital of the document i.e. agreement in this case. Minute 
reading of the agreement Ex.P-1 would show that, it primarily mentions of 
taking advance of Rs.2,21,000/- by defendant from plaintiff with an 
understanding to return it back within three months (3 months). It also 
mentions that if the defendants try to avoid re-payment within period as 
agreed, the plaintiff will have right to recover it by filing suit before Court. He 
will be liable to for cost. In the event of non-repayment of money, the plaintiff 
can take possession of house (description of which is mentioned in the 
agreement), got it registered through Court.

13.
The primary nature of document Ex.P-1 is an agreement to refund 
money obtained as loan. In pleading of plaint, such fact is mentioned and 
further main relief is for refund of money and alternate relief is of getting the 
sale deed executed.

14.
From the aforementioned facts and circumstances of case, discussions 
made above, it is apparent that plaintiff proved its case that agreement was 
executed between two at the time of obtaining loan/help of Rs.2,21,000/- and 
the trial Court recording that house was possessed jointly by defendant along 
with his brother has chosen to grant other relief as prayed for in the suit of 
refund of loan amount against the loan obtained by defendant No.1, which in 
the opinion of this Court, cannot be said to be erroneous. Judgment and 
decree passed by learned trial Court is on proper appreciation of evidence, 
hence, it does not call for any interference.
8 / 8

15.
For the foregoing discussions, I do not find any merit in this appeal and 
hence, it is dismissed.

16.
Let a decree be drawn accordingly.

1.
The Petitioner has challenged the order dated 19.1.2018 whereby
in a suo motu revision the Additional Director General of Police
(CAF) has set aside the order passed by Respondent
No.4/Inspector General of Police (CAF-1) by which after being
satisfied with the reply filed by the Petitioner he has exonerated
him from the charges levelled against him.

2.
It was argued by Learned Counsel appearing for the Petitioner
that a suo motu order was passed vide Regulation 270 of the
Chhattisgarh Police Regulations. However, the impugned order
does not disclose any reason for entertaining review under the
aforementioned Regulation of the Chhattisgarh Police
Regulations. No reason, much more plausible reason has been
assigned by the Additional Director General of Police whereby he
has directed for a departmental inquiry and has passed order that
within one month the departmental inquiry may be completed. The
Petitioner being aggrieved by the said order has filed the instant
writ petition and this Court vide order dated 2.2.2018 has passed
order that the effect and operation of the impugned order shall
remain stayed.

3.
Learned Counsel for the Petitioner further submitted that though
the departmental inquiry was not initiated against the Petitioner
3
after framing charges levelled against the Petitioner when the
notices were issued, the Petitioner has filed his reply upon which
after due consideration and after being satisfied with the reply, the
Inspector General of Police has dropped the proceedings and for
suo motu taking cognizance by the revisional authority under
Regulation 270(4) of the Chhattisgarh Police Regulations specific
reasons are required to be mentioned which is lacking in this
case.

4.
On the other hand, Learned Counsel appearing for the State
submitted that specific reasons have been assigned in the order
stating that the charges levelled against the Petitioner are serious
in nature and, therefore, the departmental inquiry was required to
be conducted.

5.
I have heard the rival contentions put-forth on behalf of the parties
and perused the material available and also gone through the
impugned order dated 19.1.2018 by which under suo motu
revision the Additional Director General of Police has set aside the
order of the Inspector General of Police/Respondent No.4 and has
directed for initiation of the departmental inquiry.

6.
From perusal of the impugned order dated 19.1.2018 it does not
seem that any specific reason has been assigned to show that
suo motu revisional power is required to be exercised by the
authorities concerned. Nothing is brought on record to prima facie
4
show that any illegality has been committed or any rules have
been violated by not deciding the issue by the Inspector General
of Police and such order cannot be passed. This Court, while
deciding a case on 24.3.2017 in Writ Appeal No.263 of 2016
(Kamlesh Kumar v. State of Chhattisgarh) [2017 (3) CGLJ 147
(DB)], has held that the authority concerned will ensure that
further proceedings are carried in strict conformity with Regulation
270 of the M.P. Police Regulations as it stood at the relevant time,
and, if any further proceedings are directed to be held after
hearing the delinquent, those proceedings shall also be held in
strict conformity of those Regulations which were applicable.

7.
In the present case, neither any opportunity of hearing was
afforded nor any notice was issued before initiation of the
departmental inquiry and a direct suo motu revisional order was
passed without assigning any reason which is apparently bad in
law, as such I deem it appropriate to set aside the impugned order
dated 19.1.2018 passed by the revisional authority, which, in my
considered opinion, is not in accordance with law.

8.
In the result, the writ petition is allowed.
