11.
In the case of Bal Thackrey (supra), earlier decisions in the case of P.N.
Duda and State of Kerala vs. M.S. Mani and others (supra) was followed.

12.
In view of decision in the case of P.N. Duda (supra) with regard to
procedure to be followed, as observed in para 54 thereof, it is clear that in the
present case, the matter was not placed before Hon’ble the Chief Justice before
filing the contempt petition. Therefore, it has to be held that the petition has
been filed without compliance of the directives as contained in the resolutions of
the Full Court dated 12/12/2006 as also direction issued by the Supreme Court
in the case of  P. N. Duda (supra). It is also relevant to mention that at the time,
this petition was filed, Chhattisgarh High Court Rules, 2005, were in force and
Rules 362 to 380 were framed in exercise of powers under the Contempt of
Courts Act, 1971. These rules were not amended to incorporate the direction
issued in the case of P. N. Duda (supra), which were subsequently reiterated in
the case of Bal Thackrey (supra). 
Even otherwise, after going through various publications made, we find
that there are statements issued alleging that attempts are being made to
influence the Court proceedings. Amongst the publications, which have been
made and whatever submissions have been made, appear to be intended to
level allegations that attempts are being made to influence the judicial
proceedings. However, beyond that, there is no specific allegation that the Court
is acting under the influence of anybody. During the course of arguments before
this Court, referring to the averments made in the affidavit in response to the
contempt petition, learned counsel appearing for the respective respondents
has stated that respondents have expressed highest regard to the authority of
this Court and the statements which were issued by the respondent No.1 and
published in the newspaper of respondents No.5 & 6 have only stated that
certain persons are attempting to influence the Court proceedings, but they
never intended much less stated any where that Courts were acting under such
7
influence. It is stated that by filing their reply, this fact has been clearly stated by
each of the respondents.

13.
Though, we find that while issuing various public statements, allegations
are mostly related to attempts made to influence judicial proceedings, it falls
short of any specific allegations against the judicial institution. At the same time,
we are also find that other statements have also been made, but, in view of
what has been stated before this Court in the affidavits filed by the respective
respondents, we are satisfied and accept the submissions made by learned
counsel for the respondents. We, however, express that due care and caution
should always be taken while making any public statement that it does not
partake the nature of equivocal statement. The respondent No.1 is expected to
be more careful and cautious in future.

14.
In the result, we are not inclined to proceed further in this matter as there
are no sufficient ground for initiating contempt proceedings against the
respondents.

15.
Accordingly, the contempt petition is closed.

10.Three classic requirements of adverse possession
are contained in nec vi, nec clam and nec
precario 
namely, adequate in continuity,
adequate in publicity and adverse to a
competitor, respectively. 
 The above-stated
requirements are required to be pleaded and
established to get a decree on the basis of
adverse possession.

11. The Supreme Court in the matter of Karnataka
Board of Wakf v. Government of India and others2
laid down the principles of law which a person
claiming adverse possession should demonstrate
by holding that a person who claims adverse
possession should show: (a) on what date he came
into possession, (b) what was the nature of his
possession, (c) whether the factum of possession
was known to the other party, (d) how long his
possession has continued, and (e) his possession
was open and undisturbed.  Their Lordships
further held that a person pleading adverse
possession has no equities in his favour.  Since
he is trying to defeat the rights of the true
2 (2004) 10 SCC 779
8
owner, it is for him to clearly plead and
establish all facts necessary to establish his
adverse possession.

12.
The principle of law laid down in Karnataka
Board of Wakf (supra) has been followed with
approval in Ravinder Kaur Grewal (supra) and
their Lordships in paragraphs 60, 61 & 62 of the
report laid down the principles and clearly held
that the adverse possession requires all the
three classic requirements to co-exist at the
same time, namely, nec vi i.e. adequate in
continuity, nec clam i.e. adequate in publicity
and nec precario i.e. adverse to a competitor,
in detail of title and his knowledge, and
observed as under: -
“60. The adverse possession requires all
the three classic requirements to co-exist
at the same time, namely, nec vi i.e.
adequate in continuity, nec clam i.e.
adequate in publicity and nec precario
i.e. adverse to a competitor, in denial of
title and his knowledge. 
 Visible,
notorious and peaceful so that if the
owner does not take care to know notorious
facts, knowledge is attributed to him on
the basis that but for due diligence he
would have known it. Adverse possession
cannot be decreed on a title which is not
pleaded.  Animus possidendi under hostile
colour of title is required.  Trespasser’s
long possession is not synonymous with
adverse
 
possession.
 
 
Trespasser’s
possession is construed to be on behalf of
9
the owner, the casual user does not
constitute adverse possession.  The owner
can take possession from a trespasser at
any point in time.  Possessor looks after
the property, protects it and in case of
agricultural property by and large the
concept is that actual tiller should own
the land who works by dint of his hard
labour and makes the land cultivable.  The
legislature in various States confers
rights based on possession.

61.
Adverse possession is heritable and
there can be tacking of adverse possession
by two or more persons as the right is
transmissible one.  In our opinion, it
confers a perfected right which cannot be
defeated on re-entry except as provided in
Article 65 itself.  Tacking is based on
the fulfillment of certain conditions,
tacking may be by possession by the

that person must be claiming through whom

62.

cannot be ousted by another person except

possessory owner acquires right, title and
interest possessed by the outgoing

consequence is that once the right, title
or interest is acquired it can be used as

restoration of possession in case of

remediless.

possession in the following terms: (Pilla
Akkayyamma case4, SCC OnLine Kar Para 27)
“27.
The
 
concept
 
of
 
adverse
possession contemplates a hostile
possession i.e. a possession which is
expressly or impliedly in denial of the
title of the true owner. Possession to
be adverse must be possession by a
person, who does not acknowledge
others’ rights but denies them.
Possession implies dominion and control
and the consciousness in the mind of
the person having dominion over an
object that he has it and can exercise
it.  Mere possession of the land would
not ripen into possessory title.
Possessor must have animus possidendi
and hold the land adverse to the title
of the true owner. Occupation only
implies bare use of the land without any
right to retain it.  In order to
constitute adverse possession, there
must be actual possession of a person
claiming as of right by himself or by
persons deriving title from him.  To
prove title to the land by adverse
possession, it is not sufficient to
show that some acts of possession have
been done.  The possession required
must be adequate in continuity, in
publicity and in extent to show that it
4 Pilla Akkayyamma v. Channnappa, 2015 SCC OnLine Kar 8226 : ILR 2015 Kar 3841
13
is adverse to the owner.  In other
words, the possession must be actual,
visible,
 
exclusive,
 
hostile
 
and
continued during the time necessary to
create a bar under the statute of
limitation.

30.
In a suit falling under Article
65 of the Limitation Act, plaintiff must
establish his title to the property.  He
need not prove that he was in possession
within 12 years.  If he fails to prove
his title, the suits fails, and the
question of adverse possession does not
arise in such a case.  When the
plaintiff has established his title to a
land, the burden of proving that he has
lost that title by reason of the adverse
possession of the defendant lies upon
the defendant.  If the defendant fails
to prove that he has been in adverse
possession for more than 12 years, the
plaintiff is entitled to succeed simply
on the strength of his title. A person
alleging that he has become owner of
immovable property by adverse possession
must establish that he was in possession
of the property peaceably, openly and in
assertion of a title hostile to the real
owner.  Stricter proof is required to
establish acquisition of title by
adverse possession for the statutory
period.”  
(emphasis supplied)

1155.
In
 Ravinder Kaur Grewal v.
Manjit Kaur5, a three-Judge Bench of this
Court of which one of us, Abdul Nazeer,
J. was a part, further developed the law
on adverse possession to hold that any
person who has perfected their title by
way of adverse possession, can file a
suit for restoration of possession in
case of dispossession.  In this view,
adverse possession is both a sword and a
shield. 
5 (2019) 8 SCC 729 : (2019) 4 SCC (Civ) 453
14

1156.
The plaintiffs have failed to
adopt a clear stand evidently because
they are conscious of the fact that in
pleading adverse possession, they must
necessarily
 
carry
 
the
 
burden
 
of
acknowledging the title of the person or
the entity against whom the plea of
adverse
 
possession
 
has
 
not
 
been
adequately set up in the pleadings and as
noted above, has not been put forth with
any certitude in the course of the
submissions.  Above all, it is impossible
for the plaintiffs to set up a case of
being in peaceful, open and continuous
possession of the entire property.  ...”

14.
Reverting to the facts of the present case in
light of the principles of law flowing from the
above-noticed judgments of the Supreme Court
(supra), it is quite vivid that plaintiffs in
the entire plaint did not make any averment that
defendants' father was the original title-holder
of the suit land and after him, defendants are
the title-holders of the suit land and the
possession of the plaintiffs is adverse to the
interest of the defendants. The plaintiffs
simply pleaded that Balgangadhar Rao Tilak, the
then Malguzar of village Mopka, was the
title-holder of the suit land who gave the suit
land to their father namely Sadhuram in lieu of
the service rendered to him and in that
capacity, they are in possession of the suit
15
land. Plaintiffs never admitted the title of the
defendants though they claimed declaration of
title on the basis of adverse possession by way
of filing the civil suit. In a suit for title
based on adverse possession, the plaintiffs were
required to plead that defendants are the title-
holders of the suit land and by remaining in
continuous, peaceful and undisturbed possession
of the suit land to the knowledge of the title-
holder, they have perfected their title by way
of adverse possession, as such, the pleading
regarding defendants being the title-holders of
the suit land is absolutely missing.

15.
Now, coming to the evidence of plaintiff No. 1
Siyaram Gond (P.W. - 1) in paragraph 13 it has
been stated that Balgangadhar Rao Tilak was the
owner of the suit land, being the Malguzar of
village Mopka, and the plaintiffs' father has
obtained the suit land from him and after their
father's death they are in possession of the
suit land. Likewise, in paragraph 16 as well, he
has stated that he is in possession of the land
owned by the Malguzar and not on the land owned
by the defendants. Next, P.W. - 2 Mahadev has
also maintained the fact that plaintiffs
16
obtained the land from the ex-malguzar.
Similarly, P.W. - 3 Shyam Bhau in his evidence
has also maintained the fact that plaintiffs are
in possession of the land given to them by the
Malguzar and they are not in possession of the
land owned by the defendants.

16.
Defendant No. 1 Prakashchandra (D.W. - 1) though
in paragraph 12 has admitted the fact that in
that year, plaintiffs have sown the crops in the
suit land but in paragraph 13 he has also stated
that plaintiffs have vacated the possession of
the suit land. D.W. - 2 Bhagwat has also stated
that plaintiffs are in possession of the suit
land at present and they have sown vegetables,
etc. in the suit land this year.

17.
As such, in the entire evidence, plaintiffs have
maintained the fact Balgangadhar Rao Tilak, the
then malguzar of village Mopka, was the title-
holder of the suit land who gave it to them and
thereafter, plaintiffs' father and now the
plaintiffs are in possession of the said suit
land since long. The plaintiffs have neither
admitted the title of defendants on the suit
land nor have they established that they are in
possession of the land held by the defendants as
17
in the evidence led before the Court, their
stand is that they are not in possession of the
land owned by the defendants, but they are in
possession of the land given to their father by
the ex-malguzar. Even otherwise, the admission
of the defendants and his witnesses that
plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land
since few years will not establish the plea of
adverse possession. As such, the basic
ingredients for establishing the plea of adverse
possession is absolutely missing, therefore, in
view of the aforesaid judgments rendered by the
Supreme Court (supra), the plaintiffs have
failed to plead and establish the plea of
adverse possession and in that view of the
matter, both the Courts below are absolutely
justified in dismissing the suit of the
plaintiffs holding that they have failed to
establish the plea of adverse possession,
therefore, they are not entitled for decree for
declaration of title and permanent injunction in
which I do not find any perversity or illegality
warranting interference under Section 100 of
CPC. 
18

18.
The second appeal, being devoid of merits,
deserves to be and is accordingly dismissed
leaving the parties to bear their own cost(s).

1.
The applicant has filed this criminal revision against the judgment and 
order dated 27.11.2012 passed in Criminal Appeal No. 101/2011 by 
the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Durg, District - Durg (C.G.), 
arising out of the judgment dated 28.07.2011 passed by the learned 
Judicial Magistrate First Class, Durg, District- Durg (C.G.) in Criminal 
Case No. 308/2010, whereby the learned JMFC has convicted the 
applicant for the offence under Section 34(1)(A) of the Excise Act and 
sentenced to undergo R.I. for 3 months and pay fine of Rs. 5000/-, In 
default of payment of fine, R.I. for 1 month.
2

2.
The case of the prosecution in brief is that on 01.03.2010 the Sub-
Inspector Mr. R.K. Verma was going to village Gureda for visit and he 
got a secret information from the informer that Deepak Nishad has 
kept some illegal liquor in his home, on this information, the inspector 
did raid in the house of the applicant and seized 48-48 quarter illegal 
liquour from the orchard of the revisioner’s father and police has 
registered the crime under Section 34(1)(A) of the Excise Act. The 
learned JMFC, Durg has trialed and considered the case of the 
accused and passed the judgment and conviction order dated 
28.07.2011 and sentenced him to undergo R.I. for 3 months and pay 
fine of Rs. 5000/-, in default of payment of fine, R.I. for one month. 
Against the said order, the appellant preferred appeal before the 
learned Additional Sessions Judge, Durg, which was dismissed. 
Hence, this revision.

3.
Learned counsel for the applicant submits that the impugned judgment 
is contrary to law, facts and circumstances of the case, therefore liable 
to be set-aside. The learned courts failed to appreciate that there are 
major contradiction and omission in the statement of prosecution 
witnesses, hence the warrant of conviction of the applicant is bad in 
law and the same is liable to be set-aside. Lastly, the applicant has 
already suffered the jail sentence for a period of 35 days, has already 
paid the fine amount and have faced the criminal trial for so many 
years, which meets the ends of justice.

4.
Per contra, learned Government Advocate, appearing for the 
respondent/ State, would strongly support the impugned judgment and 
submit that there is no need to interfere with the sentence. 
3

5.
I have heard learned counsel for the parties, perused the judgments of 
the trial Court and appellate Court and records of the trial Court with 
utmost circumspection.

6.
From perusal of the records, it transpires that the trial Court after 
considering the material available on record and evidence of the 
prosecution witnesses, has convicted the applicant for the offence 
under Section 34(1)(A) of the Excise Act and sentenced to undergo 
R.I. for 3 months and pay fine of Rs.5000/-, In default of payment of 
fine, R.I. for 1 month. I am of the view that the trial Court and the 
appellate Court have not committed any illegality or infirmity in 
afÏrming the conviction of the applicants for offence under Section 
34(1)(A) of the Excise Act.

7.
Now considering the question of sentence, as the applicant has faced 
the criminal trial since 2010 and thereafter more than 14 years have 
elapsed, considering the age of the applicant at present and further 
considering the fact that the applicant has already undergone almost 
35 days of jail sentence and paid the fine amount imposed by the trial 
Court, there would be no useful purpose to again send the applicant in 
jail as he has already suffered agony of criminal trial for so many 
years, that meets the ends of justice. So this Court finds it appropriate 
to reduce the sentence from R.I. for 3 months under Section 34(1)(A) 
of the Excise Act, to the period already undergone by the applicant i.e. 
35 days of jail sentence. Ordered accordingly.

9.
Let a copy of this order and the original records be transmitted to the 
trial Court concerned forthwith for necessary information and 
compliance.

29. In case of Dwarka Nath vs. ITO reported in (1965) 3 SCR

“4. We shall first take the preliminary
objection, for if we maintain it, no other
question will arise for consideration. Article
226 of the Constitution reads:  
29 / 31
“…every High Court shall have power,
throughout the territories in relation to
which it exercises jurisdiction, to issue
to any person or authority, including in
appropriate cases any Government,
within those territories directions, orders
or writs, including writs in the nature of
habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition,
quo warranto and certiorari, or any of
them, for the enforcement of any of the
rights conferred by Part III and for any
other purpose.”  
This article is couched in comprehensive
phraseology and it ex facie confers a wide
power on the High Courts to reach injustice
wherever it is found. The Constitution
designedly used a wide language in
describing the nature of the power, the
purpose for which and the person or
authority against whom it can be exercised.
It can issue writs in the nature of prerogative
writs as understood in England; but the
scope of those writs also is widened by the
use of the expression “nature”, for the said
expression does not equate the writs that
can be issued in India with those in England,
but only draws an analogy from them. That
apart, High Courts can also issue directions,
orders or writs other than the prerogative
writs. It enables the High Courts to mould
the reliefs to meet the peculiar and
complicated requirements of this country.
Any attempt to equate the scope of the
power of the High Court under Article 226 of
the Constitution with that of the English
Courts to issue prerogative writs is to
introduce the unnecessary procedural
restrictions grown over the years in a
comparatively small country like England
with a unitary form of government to a vast
country like India functioning under a federal
structure. Such a construction defeats the
30 / 31
purpose of the article itself. To say this is not
to say that the High Courts can function
arbitrarily under this Article. Some limitations
are implicit in the article and others may be
evolved to direct the article through defined
channels. This interpretation has been
accepted by this Court in Basappa v.
Nagappa [(1962) 2 SCR 169] and Irani v.
State of Madras [(1955) 1 SCR 250] .”

Constitution, has inherent power to do complete justice. Doing
complete justice is requirement of the fact situation of the
present case and held thus : 
“The mere fact that there is no provision
parallel to Article 142 relating to the High
Courts, can be no ground to think that they
have not to do complete justice, and if
moulding of relief would do complete justice
between the parties, the same cannot be
ordered. Absence of provision like Article
142 is not material. The High Courts too can
exercise power of review, which inheres in
every court of plenary jurisdiction. Power to
do complete justice also inhere in every
court, not to speak of a court of plenary
jurisdiction like a High Court.

31 / 31
“42. We are of the view that in case the

and has granted the relief which has not

of the Constitution of India is fully

2.
The cause shown in the said application is found to be sufficient, 
accordingly, I.A. No. 01 of 2024 is allowed.  Delay in preferring the

3.
The State has sought leave to appeal against the impugned 
judgment of acquittal dated 04.01.2023 passed in Sessions Trial 
No. 54/2021 by the Court of learned 1st Additional Sessions Judge, 
Kunkuri, District - Jashpur (C.G.) whereby the learned trial Court 
has acquitted the respondent No.1 from the charges punishable 
under Sections 363, 366, 376(D), 344, 506 (II) of IPC, respondent 
No.2 from the charges punishable under Sections 363, 366, 
376(D)A, 344, 506 (II) of IPC, respondent No.3 from the charges 
punishable under Sections 376(D), 344, 506 (II) of IPC and further 
respondent No.4 from the charges punishable under Section 506 
(II) of IPC in connection with Crime No. 94/2019 registered at 
Police Station, Jashpur, District – Jashpur (C.G.) holding that the 
prosecution has failed to prove the charges beyond reasonable 
doubt.

4.
The brief description of the prosecution story is that the 
prosecutrix/victim (PW-1) submitted a written complaint Ex.P-01 at 
Jashpur Police Station on 30.03.2019 to the effect that she was 
married in village Bxx District Jashpur and after that she lived in 
her in-laws' house. On 05.07.2018, between 10:00 and 11:00 pm, 
when she came out of her house for defecation, Santkumar and 
Suresh Yadav of village Mudakona, both were hiding near the 
3
house of the victim and ran and forcibly caught her and stuffed a 
cloth in her mouth and forcibly dragged her and took her to Sanna 
on their motorcycle and threatened to kill her and raped her 
forcibly one by one and after that took her to Bilaspur and kept her 
in a room for about 03 months and continuously sexually exploited 
(raped) her. Mahendra Yadav also came to Bilaspur in between 
and raped her and threatened to kill her. From there they brought 
her to Bagicha and kept her in the house of Santkumar's relative in 
village Bhitghara, Navatoli. Her maternal uncle came looking for 
her and took her away from there. After this Paltu threatened her 
that don't complain, otherwise she will not be able to live on this 
earth, if she complain too much then she will be taken to 
Rajasthan in a human vessel. Shivkumar Yadav and Ramkaran 
etc. have been told about this.

5.
On the said date itself, on the written application of the victim, a 
crime was registered in Police Station City Kotwali Jashpur under 
Crime No. 94/2019 Section 365, 366, 376 (D), 344, 506 (B) Indian 
Penal Code and First Information Report (Ex. P-02) was registered 
against the accused Suresh Yadav, Sant Kumar Yadav and 
Mahendra Yadav and the case was taken into investigation. After 
obtaining consent from the victim, written complaint (Ex.P-20) was 
sent to the Sub-Divisional Officer (Revenue) for granting 
permission for conducting the genital examination of the vcitim and 
after obtaining permission, written complaint (Ex.P-21) was sent to 
the District Medical Officer Jashpur for conducting the genital 
4
examination of the victim by a female Medical Officer and the 
report was obtained after conducting the genital examination of the 
victim.

6.
On 31.03.2019, the spot map of the incident, Ex.P-05 was 
prepared. On 01.04.2019, the complaint, Ex.P-23 was sent to the 
Judicial Magistrate First Class, Kunkuri, to record the statement of 
the victim under Section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure 
and the victim's statement was recorded.  Accused Suresh Kumar 
Yadav on 18.05.2019 at 21.30, accused Santkumar on 23.05.2019 
at 16.00, accused Mahendra Yadav on 23.05.2019 at 16.10, 
accused Paltu Yadav on 24.05.2019 at 20.40 were arrested in 
front of witnesses as per arrest sheet Exhibit P-28, 29, 30 and P31 
and their families were informed about the arrest.

7.
After due and necessary investigation, the charge-sheet was filed 
under aforementioned sections against the accused respondents 
before the Court of Chief Judicial Magistrate, Jashpur.  The case 
was committed to the Court of Sessions Judge, Jashpur, 
wherefrom, the case has been received on transfer to the Court of 
1st Additional Sessions Judge, Kunkuri, District – Jashpur for trial.

8.
The accused respondents adjured the guilt. In order to prove its 
case, the prosecution examined as may as 14 witnesses and 
exhibited 34 documents in its favour.  The accused have also 
examined 05 witnesses in their defence. 
5

9.
After appreciating the evidences on record, the learned trial Court 
did not believe the evidence proving guilt of the accused 
respondents, and therefore, acquitted the accused respondents 
from the offence charged vide impugned judgment dated 
04.01.2023 hence, present Criminal Miscellaneous Petition has 
been filed seeking leave to appeal.

10.
Mr. S.S. Baghel, learned Panel Lawyer appearing for the 
applicant/State would submit that the learned trial Court has failed 
to appreciate the evidence of victim (PW/1) and other prosecution 
witnesses, in its perspective and has succumbed to the surmises 
of the conjectures. He would further submit that learned trial Court 
is not justified by discarding the evidence of victim (PW/1) without 
there being any strong reason to discard her statement. He would 
also submit that the learned trial Court ought to have held that the 
victim did not consent for the alleged act of sexual implication by 
voluntarily willing herself and on the other hand it has been proved 
by the prosecution that, the alleged offence has been committed 
by the accused respondents forcibly. Hence, in the peculiar 
circumstances of the case it cannot be held that such consent was 
a legally valid consent said to have been given by the victim. The 
prosecution has been able to prove the conduct of the accused 
respondents by evidence of the other witnesses and victim 
(PW/1), therefore, in such circumstances the consent of victim for 
sexual act obtained by them cannot be held a legally valid 
consent.
6

11.
We have heard learned Panel Lawyer appearing for the 
applicant/State and perused the record of the case including the 
impugned judgment of acquittal.

12.
Learned 1st Additional Sessions Judge, Kunkuri District - Jashpur 
while acquitting the accused respondent has observed that 
considering the statements of the witnesses presented by the 
prosecution and the victim in the case, the statement of the victim 
does not appear to be natural and reliable. It does not appear that 
the victim has protested anywhere. It is said that the victim was 
taken to Bilaspur by bus and not by a private vehicle, but the 
victim has not protested anywhere. Even after the victim was 
found with the accused, no report has been filed nor has any 
report been filed regarding her disappearance, which clearly 
shows that the victim had gone with the accused voluntarily and 
that is why her family members did not give any information to the 
police in the matter and filed a report and when the accused had 
filed a report against the victim's maternal uncle and other people 
for severely beating him, then after that the report has been filed in 
the present case. Therefore, in the above circumstances of the 
case, the statement of the victim and other witnesses is not found 
to be reliable and in the absence of reliable evidence, the accused 
have not been convicted in the pending charges.

13.
Taking into consideration the findings recorded by the learned trial 
Court, acquitting the accused/respondents from aforesaid 
7
offences, we do not find any reason to allow Criminal 
Miscellaneous Petition seeking grant of leave to appeal.

14.
Recently, applying the law governing the scope of interference in 
an appeal against acquittal, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the 
case of "State of Rajasthan Vs. Kistoora Ram" reported in 2022 
SCC OnLine SC 984, has held as follows:- 
"8. The scope of interference in an appeal against 
acquittal is very limited. Unless it is found that the 
view taken by the Court is impossible or perverse, it 
is not permissible to interfere with the finding of 
acquittal. Equally if two views are possible, it is not 
permissible to set aside an order of acquittal, merely 
because the Appellate Court finds the way of 
conviction to be more probable. The interference 
would be warranted only if the view taken is not 
possible at all."

15.
Thus, for the foregoing reasons, the Criminal Miscellaneous
Petition seeking for leave to appeal being totally devoid of merits 
the same is rejected. Consequently, the appeal also stands 
dismissed.

1.   This Petition has been filed assailing the orders dated 
13.10.2016 (Annexure P-2) and 19.03.2018 (Annexure P-3) 
whereby, the claim of the Petitioners for grant of compassionate 
appointment has been rejected on the ground that elder son of 
Petitioner No.1/elder brother of Petitioner No.2 is working on the 
post of Constable at District Kabirdham.

2.       Ms. Sharma, learned Counsel appearing for the Petitioners 
submits that the orders impugned passed by the authority are bad 
in law as though the Petitioner No.2-Omesh Singh Rajput’s elder 
brother namely Oonkar Singh Rajput was working as Constable, 
but he had started living separately with his family ever since he 
got married in the year 2011 and has not been financially 
supporting the Petitioners herein.  She further submits that 
3
husband of Petitioner No.1/father of Petitioner No.2 has died in 
harness on 13.04.2016 while working on the post of Assistant 
Platoon Commander (APC) in the Office of Respondent No.4-
Commandant, 10th Battalion and as per the policy and scheme of 
compassionate appointment framed by the State Government, 
dependent family members of a deceased Government servant, 
who dies in harness, are eligible for compassionate appointment 
and therefore, the orders impugned may be quashed.

3.        Alternatively, Shri Giri, learned State Counsel has opposed 
the submission made by learned Counsel for the Petitioners and 
submits that the issue involved in this Petition is no longer res 
integra and the same has been decided by the Full Bench of this 
Court vide order dated 21.06.2023 passed in the matter of State of 
Chhattisgarh & Ors. vs. Umesh Thakur in Writ Appeal 
No.236/2022 whereby, it has been held that compassionate 
appointment has to be granted in accordance with the policy 
applicable and the said policy clearly indicates that where one of 
the family members of the deceased Government servant is 
already in Government service, then the other members of the 
family of the deceased Government servant would not be entitled 
for compassionate appointment and therefore, the orders 
impugned do not call for any interference of this Court.
4

4.     Having considered the submissions made by learned Counsel 
for the parties and the judgment passed in State of Chhattisgarh & 
Ors. vs. Umesh Thakur (supra), this Court is of the view that there 
is no perversity or illegality in the orders impugned dated 
13.10.2016 (Annexure P-2) and 19.03.2018 (Annexure P-3) and 
the same do not warrant any interference of this Court invoking writ 
jurisdiction.

5.     Accordingly, the instant Petition is liable to be and his hereby 
dismissed.

2. By this writ petition, petitioner is challenging the legality and sustainability
of the impugned order dated 09.10.2023 (Annexure P/1) passed by the
Chhattisgarh State Information Commission, Raipur imposing penalty of
Rs. 25,000/- upon the petitioner under the provisions of Section 20 (1) of
the Right to Information Act, 2005 (hereinafter for brevity referred to as
the Act, 2005).

3. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that the petitioner was holding
the post of Panchayat Secretary, Village Panchayat Kerakachhar, Block –
Patthalgaon, District – Jashpur. Respondent No. 3 submitted an
application under the Act, 2005 for providing the information of the cash
ledger book for the period from 01.04.2020 till 31.12.2021. When the
information could not be supplied, he submitted the first appeal on
25.01.2022 and the First Appellate Authority had not passed any order in
the said appeal. Being aggrieved, the petitioner filed complaint before the
Second Appellate Authority on 27.04.2022 along with the application
dated 13.12.2021 and copy of the first appeal dated 25.01.2022 enclosing
the other supporting documents. After filing of the complaint, the
information was supplied as asked for by the Respondent No. 3 and he
also acknowledged the receipt of information on 18.01.2023 (Annexure
P/4). In the acknowledgment, he has also mentioned that he do not want
any proceedings or action on the complaint filed by him before the State
Information Commission.

4. It is contention of the counsel for the petitioner that as the applicant
seeking information has given an acknowledgment that he do not want
any action against the Public Information Officer, petitioner was of the
view that the complaint would be withdrawn or dismissed by the State
Information Commission, however, the impugned order was passed
imposing the penalty. Even after providing the information sought for. It is
contention of counsel for the petitioner that before imposing penalty, no
3
show-cause notice as provided under Section 20 (1) of the Act, 2005 was
issued to the petitioner and therefore, also, the order imposing penalty is
bad in law.

5. Learned counsel for the Respondent No. 3 submits that the reply is filed
pleading therein that the Respondent No. 3 is satisfied with the
information supplied by the petitioner and his grievance is settled.
Respondent No. 3 gave acknowledgment in this regard on 18.01.2023
(Annexure P/4). The fact of providing information as sought for giving
acknowledgment in this regard, regarding his satisfaction to the
information and further, that the Respondent No. 3 do not want any action
to the complaint could not be placed before the State Information
Commission, which led to passing of the order.

6. Learned counsel for Respondent No. 1 submits that the Respondent No.
4 has filed complaint pleading therein that the application seeking
information under the Right to Information was not supplied by the Public
Information Officer-cum-Secretary, Village Panchayat Kerkachhar, Janpad
Panchayat Patthalgaon. He contended that the complaint was registered,
show-cause notice was issued upon which, petitioner appeared before
the commission on 10.02.2023. After considering the records and
submissions made, the Commission ordered for issuance of show-cause
notice under Section 20 (1) & 20 (2) of the Act, 2005. The petitioner has
not submitted any reply to the show-cause notice and thereafter, the order
impugned was passed which is in accordance with law following the due
procedure as provided under the Act, 2005. Hence, the impugned order
dated dated 09.10.2023 (Annexure P/1) does not call for any interference.

7. I have heard learned counsel for the respective parties and also perused
the documents placed before this Court for perusal. 
4

8. Perusal of the documents enclosed would show that the Respondent No.
3 filed an application seeking information under the Act, 2005. It is also
appearing that the information was not supplied within the time as
prescribed under the Act, 2005 which led to filing of the appeal by the
Respondent No. 3 to the Appellate Authority and thereof, when after
passing of the order by the Appellate Authority of providing information, it
was not supplied to the Respondent No. 3 which made him to file a
complaint. The acknowledgment dated 18.01.2023 (Annexure P/4) would
show that during pendency of the complaint, information was supplied to
the satisfaction of the Respondent No. 3/applicant therein and he also
acknowledged the same, mentioned that he does not want to pursue the
complaint.

9. From the acknowledgment (Annexure P/4), it is appearing that the
Respondent No. 3 have clearly stated that he do not want to pursue the
complaint and made a prayer to close the file. The Respondent No.
1/Commission also submitted its reply pleading therein that the show-
cause notice under Section 20 (1) of the Act, 2005 was also directed to be
issued and further that the notices have been issued through registered
post. 
10.Be that as it may, under the provisions of the Act, 2005, the First Appellate
Authority or the State Information Commission can impose penalty and
may also directed for disciplinary action against the Public Information
Officer under Section 20 (2) of the Act, 2005. However, it is pre-condition
that before imposing penalty or passing the order of direction for initiating
departmental proceedings against the Public Information Officer, he is to
be given an opportunity of hearing. The documents placed on recorded
along with the reply filed by the Respondent No. 1/Commission would
show that the Respondent No. 1 has filed a copy of the notice of
complaint as Annexure R-01/01 and further, the copy of the order-sheets
5
dated 10.02.2023 as Annexure R-01/03. On the right-hand side corner, it
is mentioned “issued on 08.09.2023”. Perusal of the order-sheet would
show that in compliance of the order dated 10.02.2023, show-cause
notice under Section 20 (1) and 20 (2) may have been issued on
08.09.2023. 
11.In reply, it is pleaded that the show-cause notice was issued by registered
post. The notice is to be sent on the address of the petitioner who is
posted in the village in rural area. No document has been enclosed to
show that the show-cause notice, if issued on 08.09.2023, was served
upon the petitioner before the date fixed i.e. 09.10.2023. 
12.The order of penalty for failure to provide information is akin to criminal
action to be taken against a person under the law and therefore, it was
the duty cast upon the Commission to record that the notice issued for
imposing penalty and taking disciplinary action is served upon the person
to whom it is issued i.e. the petitioner and even after service of notice, he
failed to appear and submit its reply. In the impugned order dated
09.10.2023, no such finding is recorded by the Respondent No.
1/Commission. In absence of such specific finding recorded by the
Commission before passing an order of imposing penalty under Section
20 (1) of Act, 2005 that the show-cause notice ordered to be issued by the
Commission was issued and served upon the Public Information Officer,
more so, when in the order-sheet pursuant to the order dated 10.02.2023,
the date of issuance is as reflecting only on 08.09.2023 i.e. more than 07
months from the date of order. Service of notice cannot be presumed.
Respondent No. 2 has not filed any document in support of its contention
to show that notice if any, issued by what mode and whether it is served
upon prior to date of hearing. It is mandatory that before imposing penalty
or passing the order of direction for initiating departmental proceedings
6
against the Public Information Officer, he is required to be given an
opportunity of hearing.

13. In the aforementioned facts of the case, as there is no material available
in the record or placed before the Respondent No. 1 to satisfy that the
notice served issued and served upon the petitioner before the date of
hearing of the case. The impugned order dated 09.10.2023 (Annexure
P/1) imposing penalty upon the petitioner under Section 20 (1) is in
violation of principles of natural justice.

14. For the foregoing discussion, order impugned dated 09.10.2023
(Annexure P/1) imposing penalty upon the petitioner is not sustainable in
the eyes of law. Accordingly, it is set-aside. 
15.The writ petition stands allowed.

notice and thereafter, the order impugned was passed which is in

7. I have heard learned counsel for the respective parties and also perused
the documents placed before this Court for perusal.

8. Perusal of the documents enclosed would show that the Respondent No.
3 filed an application seeking information under the Act, 2005. It is also
appearing that the information was not supplied within the time as
prescribed under the Act, 2005 which led to filing of the appeal by the
Respondent No. 3 to the Appellate Authority and thereafter, when even
after passing of the order by the Appellate Authority of providing
information, it was not supplied to the Respondent No. 3, he filed
complaint. Perusal of the document Annexure P/4  would show that during
pendency of the complaint, information was supplied to the Respondent
No. 3/applicant therein to his satisfaction which was also acknowledged
by him. In the acknowledgment, it is also mentioned that he does not want
to pursue the complaint.

9. From the acknowledgment (Annexure P/4), it is appearing that the
Respondent No. 3 have clearly stated that he do not want to pursue the
complaint and made a prayer to close the file. 
10.Be that as it may, under the provisions of the Act, 2005 it is an obligation
on the part of the Public Information Officer to provide an information as
sought for by the applicant under the provisions of the Act, 2005, except
the information which falls within the provision under Section 8 of the Act,

11. Section 20 of the Act, 2005 provides for the penalties to be imposed upon
the Public Information Officer by the State Information Commission. While
deciding the complaint or appeal, if in the opinion of the Information
Commission or the Appellate Authority, the Public Information Officer
without any reasonable cause refuses to receive an application for
5 / 6
information or has not furnished the information within the time specified,
penalty can be imposed, however, under the provisions of the Act, 2005, it
is mandatory upon the authority imposing penalty to give reasonable
opportunity of being heard before any penalty is imposed upon him. Copy
of the order-sheet dated 25.01.2023 filed as Annexure R-01/3 would show
that the Commission has ordered for issuance of notice under Section 20
(1) and 20 (2) of the Act, 2005 to the petitioner/Public Information Officer.

and date is 22.08.2023”. Pursuant to order dated 25.01.2023, as per the
noting made in the order-sheet, it is appearing that the notice was issued
after about 07 months i.e. only on 22.08.2023, the order impugned is
passed thereafter on 22.09.2023.

action to be taken against a person under the law and therefore, it was
the duty cast upon the Commission to record that the notice issued for
imposing penalty and taking disciplinary action is served upon the person
to whom it is issued i.e. the petitioner and even after service of notice, he
failed to appear and submit its reply. In the impugned order dated
28.11.2023, no such finding is recorded by the Respondent No.
2/Commission. In absence of such specific finding recorded by the
Commission before passing an order of imposing penalty under Section
20 (1) of Act, 2005 that the show-cause notice ordered to be issued by the
Commission was issued and served upon the Public Information Officer,
more so, when in the order-sheet pursuant to the order dated 25.01.2023,
the date of issuance is as reflecting only on 22.08.2023 i.e. more than 07
months from the date of order. Issuance and service of notice cannot be
presumed. Respondent No. 2 has not filed any document in support of its
contention to show that notice if any, issued by what mode and whether it
is served upon prior to date of hearing. It is mandatory that before
6 / 6
imposing penalty or passing the order of direction for initiating
departmental proceedings against the Public Information Officer, he is
required to be given an opportunity of hearing. 
13.For the foregoing discussion, the order impugned dated 22.09.2023
(Annexure P/1) imposing penalty upon the petitioner is not sustainable in

14.The writ petition stands allowed.

details of bank accounts, list of beneficiaries of the villages which have
been declared ODF. When the information could not be supplied, he
submitted the first appeal and the First Appellate Authority vide its order
dated 10.01.2022 directed to provide the information. According to the
facts as reflecting from the impugned order, the information could not be
supplied and therefore, the complaint was filed by the Respondent No. 3.
After filing of the complaint, the information was supplied as asked for by
the Respondent No. 3 and he also acknowledged the receipt of
information on 18.01.2023 (Annexure P/4). In the acknowledgment, he
has also mentioned that he do not want any proceedings or action on the
complaint filed by him before the State Information Commission.

4. It is contention of the counsel for the petitioner that as the applicant
seeking information has given an acknowledgment that he do not want
any action against the Public Information Officer, petitioner was of the
view that the complaint would be withdrawn or dismissed by the State
Information Commission, however, the impugned order was passed
imposing the penalty. Even after providing the information sought for. It is
3
contention of counsel for the petitioner that before imposing penalty, no
show-cause notice as provided under Section 20 (1) of the Act, 2005 was
issued to the petitioner and therefore, also, the order imposing penalty is
bad in law.

5. Learned counsel for the Respondent No. 3 submits that the reply is filed
pleading therein that the Respondent No. 3 is satisfied with the
information supplied by the petitioner and his grievance is settled.
Respondent No. 3 gave acknowledgment in this regard on 18.01.2023.
The fact of providing information as sought for giving acknowledgment in
this regard, regarding his satisfaction to the information and further, that
the Respondent No. 3 do not want any action to the complaint could not
be placed before the State Information Commission, which led to passing
of the order.

6. Learned counsel for Respondents No. 1 submits that the Respondent No.
1 has filed reply pleading therein that the application seeking information
under the Right to Information was refused to be accepted by the Public
Information Officer-cum-Secretary, Village Panchayat Garjiyabathan,
Janpad Panchayat Patthalgaon against which, appeal was preferred. The
First Appellate Authority directed to provide the requisite information free
of cost but, even then, information was not supplied and thereafter, a
complaint was filed by the Respondent No. 3. He contended that the
complaint was registered, show-cause notice was issued upon which,
petitioner appeared before the commission on 24.01.2023. After
considering the records and submissions made, the Commission ordered
for issuance of show-cause notice under Section 20 (1) & 20 (2) of the
Act, 2005. The petitioner has not submitted any reply to the show-cause
notice and thereafter, the order impugned was passed which is in
accordance with law following the due procedure as provided under the
4
Act, 2005. Hence, the impugned order dated dated 21.09.2023 (Annexure
P/1) does not call for any interference.

7. I have heard learned counsel for the respective parties and also perused
the documents placed before this Court for perusal.

8. Perusal of the documents enclosed would show that the Respondent No.
3 filed an application seeking information under the Act, 2005. It is also
appearing that the information was not supplied within the time as
prescribed under the Act, 2005 which led to filing of the complaint by the
Respondent No. 3 to the Appellate Authority and thereafter, when even
after passing of the order by the Appellate Authority of providing
information, it was not supplied to the Respondent No. 3, he filed
complaint. Perusal of the document Annexure P/4  would show that during
pendency of the appeals, information was supplied to the Respondent No.
3/applicant therein to his satisfaction which was also acknowledged by
him. In the acknowledgment, it is also mentioned that he does not want to
pursue the complaint.

9. From the acknowledgment (Annexure P/4), it is appearing that the
Respondent No. 3 have clearly stated that he do not want to pursue the
complaint and made a prayer to close the file. 
10.Be that as it may, under the provisions of the Act, 2005 it is an obligation
on the part of the Public Information Officer to provide an information as
sought for by the applicant under the provisions of the Act, 2005, except
the information which falls within the provision under Section 8 of the Act,

11. Section 20 of the Act, 2005 provides for the penalties to be imposed upon
the Public Information Officer by the State Information Commission. While
deciding the complaint or appeal, if in the opinion of the Information
5
Commission or the Appellate Authority, the Public Information Officer
without any reasonable cause refuses to receive an application for
information or has not furnished the information within the time specified,
penalty can be imposed, however, under the provisions of the Act, 2005, it
is mandatory upon the authority imposing penalty to give reasonable
opportunity of being heard before any penalty is imposed upon him. Copy
of the order-sheet dated 24.01.2023 filed as Annexure R-01/2 would show
that the Commission has ordered for issuance of notice under Section 20
(1) and 20 (2) of the Act, 2005 to the petitioner/Public Information Officer.
In the right hand corner of the order-sheet, there is mentioned “issued
and date is 28.08.2023”. Pursuant to order dated 24.01.2023, as per the
noting made in the order-sheet, it is appearing that the notice was issued
after about 07 months i.e. only on 28.08.2023, the order impugned is
passed thereafter on 21.09.2023.

12. The order of penalty for failure to provide information is akin to criminal
action to be taken against a person under the law and therefore, it was
the duty cast upon the Commission to record that the notice issued for
imposing penalty and taking disciplinary action is served upon the person
to whom it is issued i.e. the petitioner and even after service of notice, he
failed to appear and submit its reply. In the impugned order dated
21.09.2023, no such finding is recorded by the Respondent No.
1/Commission. In absence of such specific finding recorded by the
Commission before passing an order of imposing penalty under Section
20 (1) of Act, 2005 that the show-cause notice ordered to be issued by the
Commission was issued and served upon the Public Information Officer,
more so, when in the order-sheet pursuant to the order dated 24.01.2023,
the date of issuance is as reflecting only on 28.08.2023 i.e. more than 07
months from the date of order. Issuance and service of notice cannot be
presumed. Respondent No. 2 has not filed any document in support of its
6
contention to show that notice if any, issued by what mode and whether it
is served upon prior to date of hearing. It is mandatory that before
imposing penalty or passing the order of direction for initiating
departmental proceedings against the Public Information Officer, he is
required to be given an opportunity of hearing. 
13.For the foregoing discussion, the order impugned dated 21.09.2023
(Annexure P/1) imposing penalty upon the petitioner is not sustainable in
the eyes of law. Accordingly, it is set-aside. 
14.The writ petition stands allowed.

1. These Revisions are directed against the judgment dated 29.10.2010
passed by the Additional Sessions Judge, (FTC) Dhamtari in Criminal
Appeal No.72/2010, affirming the judgment dated 21.9.2010 passed by
the Judicial Magistrate 1st Class, Dhamtari in Criminal Case
No.67/2008, whereby the learned Judicial Magistrate 1st Class has
convicted the applicants for offence under Section 420, 471, 420/34 &
471/34 of the IPC and sentenced each of them to undergo RI for 2 years
and to pay a fine of Rs.1000/-, in default of payment of fine to further
undergo SI for 1 month and to undergo RI for 3 years & to pay a fine of
Rs.1,000/-, in default of payment of fine to further undergo SI for 1
month, respectively.

2. The prosecution case, in brief, is that Amit Jain (complainant) owns an
agency namely, Scooter House at Dhamri and he is engaged in the
business of selling two wheelers of TVS company.   On 1.1.2009, the
complainant sold one TVS Scooty to one Pradeep Chandrakar, who is
the resident of Bhatapara, Tehsil Kurud.  On 7.1.2009 & 16.1.2009, the
said Pradeep Chandrakar came along with his friends namely, Hemant
Thakur and Lokesh Kumar Sahu to the agency of the complainant.  For
Hemant Thakur, one TVS two wheeler was purchased in respect of
which Bill No.701 was issued and the complainant was to receive a sum
of Rs.11,730/- towards down payment, which was to be paid by said
Hemant Thakur.  Likewise, one Scooty Pep was also purchased for
Lokesh Sahu, who is said to be resident of Tehsil Kurud, which respect
of which also Bill No.770 was issued.  However, when the down
3
payment was not made by said Hemant Thakur, the complainant tried to
contact him on the phone number given by him, but his phone was
switched off.  When the complainant verified his address, he came to
know that no such person was residing on the said address.  Thereafter,
in the similar fashion, the complainant tried to contact the said Pradeep
Chandrakar and Lokesh Kumar Sahu on their respective address and
number, but their whereabouts could not be traced.  Therefore, the
complainant lodged a written complaint with the concerned Police
Station, on the basis of which the FIR (Ex.-P/2) was registered. After
completion of investigation, charge-sheet was filed before the
competent Court against the applicants.

3. The learned Judicial Magistrate 1st Class after appreciating oral and
documentary evidence available on record vide judgment dated
21.9.2010 convicted and sentenced the applicants as mentioned in
opening paragraph of this order.

4. Against the said judgment,  the applicants have preferred Criminal
Appeal before the Additional Sessions Judge, (FTC) Dhamrtari who by
the impugned judgment dated 29.10.2010 affirmed the conviction and
sentence passed by the Judicial Magistrate 1st Class, Dhamtari. Hence,
these criminal revisions.

5. At the outset, learned counsel for the applicants would submit that
applicant - Jhammanlal Yadav in CRR No.680/2010 has died and no
4
application has been filed by the legal heirs of the said applicant to
prosecute this revision on his behalf.

6. In the circumstances, the said Revision in respect of applicant No.1 –
Jhammanlal Yadav is abated.  Learned counsel for the applicant is
directed to carry out amendment during the course of the day.

7. Learned counsel for the applicants further submit that the judgments of
the Court below are bad in law as well as on facts. The learned Court
below ought not to have convicted and sentenced the applicants.  In
alternative, they would submit that applicant Dhavendra Kumar in CRR
No.7/2011 has already completed the jail sentence of 22 months & 2
days and other applicants namely, Kishore Kumar and Manoj Kumar
have also completed the jail sentence of 19 months.  Therefore,  ends of
justice would be met if the applicants are sentenced to the period
already undergone by them, as the applicants are suffering the agony of
criminal case for more than 14 years since the incident happened in the
year 2009.

8. Per contra, learned State Counsel submit that both the Courts below
have rightly appreciated the evidence and conviction and sentence
awarded by the Court below are just and proper which do not call for
any interference.

9. I have heard learned counsel for the parties at length and perused the
records with utmost circumspection. 
5

10. (PW-1) Amit Jain (complainant) has stated in his evidence that he is
running the agency for selling TVS two wheelers.  His showroom was
situated near Gujrati Colony, Dhamtari.  The accused persons
impersonated themselves and produced forged Ration card and papers
and got financed 3 TVS vehicles on 1.1.2009, 7.1.2009 & 16.1.2009.
The said vehicles were financed through Astha Finance, RD Finance
and SK Finance.  Though the financiers have paid the entire amount to
him, but when the installments were not recovered, it came to his notice
that the said fraud has been committed by the accused persons in a
planned manner.  So, the complainant has lodged the written complaint
(Ex.-P/1) at PS City Kotwali, Dhamtari, based on which the FIR (Ex.-P/
2) was registered by ASI BR Sinha against 3 persons namely, Hemant,
Pradeep Chandrakar and Lokesh Sahu.  During investigation, it was
revealed that in the fake names of Pradeep Chandrakar, Hemant Thakur
and Lokesh Sahu, the present applicants have produced fake documents
like ration card and other papers at the showroom of the complainant
and successfully got financed all the 3 vehicles.  During investigation,
on the basis of memorandum (Ex.-P/4 to P/7), the said vehicles which
were sold to other persons were recovered vide Ex.-P/8 to P/10.

11. (PW-2) Sharad Choubey, was working as salesman at the showroom of
the complainant with whom the IO has seized receipt No.686, Article
‘C’; receipt No.701, Article ‘D’ and receipt No.717, Article ‘E’, through
seizure memo (Ex.-P/3) and the accused persons by impersonating
6
themselves as Pradeep Chandrakar, Hemant Thakur and Lokesh Sahu,
in a fraudulent manner, purchased the said vehicles.

12. (PW-3) Manoj Rathi, an employee of the Astha Finance, has
categorically stated that though the said accused persons have pasted
their own original photographs, but they have furnished the details of
other persons and during investigation, in front of him, when accused
Dhavendra Kumar was interrogated by the police, the whole conspiracy
came to the fore and the vehicles which were financed in a fraudulent
manner were also seized from their possession.

13. In view of the above, it appears that the accused persons had used
forged documents like ration card, certificates, photographs etc. and by
way of impersonation, they got financed the said two wheelers from the
showroom of the complainant and also induced the financier/salesman
and in a fraudulent manner sold the said vehicles to other persons and
cheated the complainant.  So, the offence under Sections 420 & 471 of
the IPC was rightly proved by the prosecution and this Court does not
find any illegality or infirmity in the impugned judgments of the Courts
below.  The conviction is well merited which is affirmed.

14. So far as sentence part is concerned, the applicants have been awarded
maximum sentence of 3 years, the incident happened in the year 2009
and more than 14 years have elapsed, therefore, this Court is of the view
that ends of justice would be served if the applicants are sentenced to
the period already undergone by them.  Ordered accordingly.
7

15. However, the fine amount of Rs.1,000/- imposed by the Court below for
offence under Sections 420 & 471 of the IPC requires to be enhanced.
Accordingly, it is ordered that the applicants shall pay fine amount of
Rs.2,000/- on each count and thereby, the applicants shall pay fine
amount of Rs.3,000/- for offence under Sections 420/34 & 471/34 of the
IPC separately.    The aforesaid enhanced fine amount on both counts
i.e. Rs.2,000/- & Rs.2,000/-, in aggregate Rs.4,000/-, would be
deposited by the applicants within a further period of 2 months, failing
which the applicants shall suffer RI for 1 month.

16. With the aforesaid modifications, the Criminal Revisions are partly
allowed to the extent indicated herein-above.

17. Let a copy of this order and the original records be sent to the trial court
concerned forthwith for necessary information and compliance.

be deem fit in the given facts and circumstances of
the instant case.”

2. By this writ petition, petitioner is challenging the legality and sustainability
of the impugned order dated 24.11.2023 (Annexure P/1) passed by the
Chhattisgarh State Information Commission, Raipur imposing penalty of
Rs. 25,000/- upon the petitioner under the provisions of Section 20 (1) of
the Right to Information Act, 2005 (hereinafter for brevity referred to as
the Act, 2005).

3. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that the petitioner was holding
the post of Panchayat Secretary, Village Panchayat Ila, Block –
Patthalgaon, District – Jashpur. Respondent No. 4 submitted an
application under the Act, 2005 for providing the information of funds
received and expended under the Swachh Bharat Mission (Rural), the
details of bank accounts, list of beneficiaries of the villages which have
been declared ODF. When the information could not be supplied, he
submitted the first appeal on 20.12.2021 and the First Appellate Authority
had not passed any order in the said appeal. Being aggrieved, the
petitioner filed complaint before the Commission on 01.04.2022. After
filing of the complaint, the information was supplied as asked for by the
Respondent No. 4 and he also acknowledged the receipt of information
on 28.12.2022 (Annexure P/4). In the acknowledgment, he has also
mentioned that he do not want any proceedings or action on the
complaint filed by him before the State Information Commission.

4. It is contention of the counsel for the petitioner that as the applicant
seeking information has given an acknowledgment that he do not want
any action against the Public Information Officer, petitioner was of the
view that the complaint would be withdrawn or dismissed by the State
Information Commission, however, the impugned order was passed
3
imposing the penalty, even after providing the information sought for. It is
contention of counsel for the petitioner that before imposing penalty, no
show-cause notice as provided under Section 20 (1) of the Act, 2005 was
issued to the petitioner and therefore, also, the order imposing penalty is
bad in law.

5. Learned counsel for the Respondent No. 4 submits that the reply is filed
pleading therein that the Respondent No. 4 is satisfied with the
information supplied by the petitioner and his grievance is settled.
Respondent No. 4 gave acknowledgment in this regard on 28.12.2022
(Annexure P/4). The fact of providing information as sought for giving
acknowledgment in this regard, regarding his satisfaction to the
information and further, that the Respondent No. 4 do not want any action
to the complaint could not be placed before the State Information
Commission, which led to passing of the order.

6. Learned counsel for Respondent No. 2 submits that the Respondent No.
4 has filed complaint pleading therein that he submitted an application on
08.11.2021 seeking information under the Act, 2005 which was not
supplied within the stipulated period as provided under the Act, 2005.
Respondent No. 4 thereafter preferred first appeal before the First
Appellate Authority, however, the First Appellate Authority has also not
taken decision and not passed any order in the first appeal which made
the Respondent No. 4 to file complaint before the Respondent No. 2
which was registered. He contended that the Respondent No. 2 in its
proceedings dated 21.08.2023 has directed for issuance of show-cause
notice under Section 20 (1) & 20 (2) of the Act, 2005 stating as to why
cost of Rs. 25,000/- be not imposed and as to why, the disciplinary
proceedings be not initiated and on the next date fixed, the impugned
order was passed. Taking note of the fact that the reply to the show-cause
4
notice was also not filed, the order impugned is passed following the due
procedure as provided under the Act, 2005.

7. I have heard learned counsel for the respective parties and also perused
the documents placed before this Court for perusal.

8. Perusal of the documents enclosed would show that the Respondent No.
4 filed an application seeking information under the Act, 2005. It is also
appearing that the information was not supplied within the time as
prescribed under the Act, 2005 which led to filing of the appeal by the
Respondent No. 4 to the Appellate Authority. The Appellate Authority has
also not taken decision on the first appeal. Respondent No. 4 filed a
complaint. The acknowledgment dated 28.12.2022 (Annexure P/4) would
show that during pendency of the complaint, information was supplied to
the satisfaction of the Respondent No. 4/applicant therein and he also
acknowledged the same, mentioned that he does not want to pursue the
complaint.

9. From the acknowledgment (Annexure P/4), it is appearing that the
Respondent No. 4 have clearly stated that he do not want to pursue the
appeal and made a prayer to close the file. The Respondent No.
2/Commission also submitted its reply pleading therein that the show-
cause notice under Section 20 (1) of the Act, 2005 was also directed to be
issued and further that the notices have been issued through registered
post. 
10.Be that as it may, under the provisions of the Act, 2005, the First Appellate
Authority or the State Information Commission can impose penalty and
may also directed for disciplinary action against the Public Information
Officer under Section 20 (2) of the Act, 2005. However, it is pre-condition
that before imposing penalty or passing the order of direction for initiating
departmental proceedings against the Public Information Officer, he is to
5
be given an opportunity of hearing. The documents placed on recorded
along with the reply filed by the Respondent No. 2/Commission would
show that the Respondent No. 2 has filed a copy of the notice of
complaint as Annexure R-01/01 and further, the copy of the order-sheets
dated 03.01.2023 as Annexure R-01/03. Perusal of the order-sheet would
show that in compliance of the order dated 03.01.2023 and 21.08.2023,
direction was issued for issuance of show-cause notice under Section 20
(1) and 20 (2) of the Act, 2005. But, in the said order-sheets, there is no
mention that pursuant to the order issued by the Respondent  No. 2,
show-cause notice was issued or was served upon the petitioner. 
11.In reply, it is pleaded that the show-cause notice was issued by registered
post. The notice is to be sent on the address of the petitioner who is
posted in the village in rural area. No document has been enclosed to
show that the show-cause notice, if issued, was served upon the
petitioner before the date fixed pursuant to the order dated 03.01.2023 i.e.
on 21.08.2023 and thereafter, pursuant to the order dated 21.08.2023 i.e.
on 24.11.2023. 
12.The order of penalty for failure to provide information is akin to criminal
action to be taken against a person under the law and therefore, it was
the duty cast upon the Commission to record that the notice issued for
imposing penalty and taking disciplinary action is served upon the person
to whom it is issued i.e. the petitioner and even after service of notice, he
failed to appear and submit its reply. In the impugned order dated
24.11.2023, no such finding is recorded by the Respondent No.
2/Commission. In absence of such specific finding recorded by the
Commission before passing an order of imposing penalty under Section
20 (1) of Act, 2005 that the show-cause notice ordered to be issued by the
Commission was issued and served upon the Public Information Officer,
more so, when in the order-sheet pursuant to the order dated 03.01.2023
6
and 21.08.2023, no date of issuance of show-cause notice is reflecting.
Issuance and service of notice cannot be presumed. Respondent No. 2
has not filed any document in support of its contention to show that notice
if any, issued by what mode and whether it is served upon prior to date of
hearing.

13. In the aforementioned facts of the case, as there is no material available
in the record to satisfy that the notice was issued and served upon the
petitioner before the date of hearing of the case. The impugned order
dated 24.11.2023 (Annexure P/1) imposing penalty upon the petitioner
under Section 20 (1) is in violation of principles of natural justice.

14. For the foregoing discussion, order impugned dated 24.11.2023
(Annexure P/1) imposing penalty upon the petitioner is not sustainable in
the eyes of law. Accordingly, it is set-aside. 
15.The writ petition stands allowed.

the Right to Information Act, 2005 (hereinafter for brevity referred to as
the Act, 2005).

3. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that the petitioner was holding
the post of Panchayat Secretary, Village Panchayat Deewanpur, Block –
Patthalgaon, District – Jashpur. Respondent No. 3 submitted an
application under the Act, 2005 for providing the information with regard to
the amount received and expended under the head of Swachh Bharat
Mission (Rural), target fixed and target achieved. When the information
could not be supplied, he submitted the first appeal on 20.12.2021 and
the First Appellate Authority had not passed any order in the said appeal.
Being aggrieved, the petitioner filed second appeal/complaint before the
Second Appellate Authority on 17.02.2022 along with the application
dated 08.11.2021. After filing of the complaint, the information was
supplied as asked for by the Respondent No. 3 and he also
acknowledged the receipt of information on 18.01.2023 (Annexure P/2). In
the acknowledgment, he has also mentioned that he do not want any
proceedings or action on the complaint filed by him before the State
Information Commission.

4. It is contention of the counsel for the petitioner that as the applicant
seeking information has given an acknowledgment that he do not want
any action against the Public Information Officer, petitioner was of the
view that the complaint would be withdrawn or dismissed by the State
Information Commission, however, the impugned order was passed
3
imposing the penalty. Even after providing the information sought for. It is
contention of counsel for the petitioner that before imposing penalty, no
show-cause notice as provided under Section 20 (1) of the Act, 2005 was
issued to the petitioner and therefore, also, the order imposing penalty is
bad in law.

5. Learned counsel for the Respondent No. 3 submits that the reply is filed
pleading therein that the Respondent No. 3 is satisfied with the
information supplied by the petitioner and his grievance is settled.
Respondent No. 3 gave acknowledgment in this regard on 18.01.2023.
The fact of providing information as sought for giving acknowledgment in
this regard, regarding his satisfaction to the information and further, that
the Respondent No. 3 do not want any action to the complaint could not
be placed before the State Information Commission, which led to passing
of the order.

6. Learned counsel for Respondent No. 1 submits that the Respondent No.
3 has filed complaint pleading therein that the application seeking
information under the Right to Information was not supplied by the Public
Information Officer-cum-Secretary, Village Panchayat Deewanpur, Janpad
Panchayat Patthalgaon. He contended that the complaint was registered,
show-cause notice was issued upon which, petitioner appeared before
the commission on 25.01.2023. After considering the records and
submissions made, the Commission ordered for issuance of show-cause
notice under Section 20 (1) & 20 (2) of the Act, 2005. The petitioner has
not submitted any reply to the show-cause notice and thereafter, the order
impugned was passed which is in accordance with law following the due
procedure as provided under the Act, 2005. Hence, the impugned order
dated dated 22.09.2023 (Annexure P/1) does not call for any interference.

7. I have heard learned counsel for the respective parties and also perused
the documents placed before this Court for perusal. 
4

8. Perusal of the documents enclosed would show that the Respondent No.
3 filed an application seeking information under the Act, 2005. It is also
appearing that the information was not supplied within the time as
prescribed under the Act, 2005 which led to filing of the appeal by the
Respondent No. 3 to the Appellate Authority and when after passing of
the order by the Appellate Authority of providing information, it was not
supplied to the Respondent No. 3 which made him to file a complaint. The
acknowledgment dated 18.01.2023 (Annexure P/2) would show that
during pendency of the second appeal, information was supplied to the
satisfaction of the Respondent No. 3/applicant therein and he also
acknowledged the same, mentioned that he does not want to pursue the
complaint.

9. From the acknowledgment (Annexure P/2), it is appearing that the
Respondent No. 3 have clearly stated that he do not want to pursue the
complaint and made a prayer to close the file. The Respondent No.
1/Commission also submitted its reply pleading therein that the show-
cause notice under Section 20 (1) of the Act, 2005 was also directed to be
issued and further that the notices have been issued through registered
post. 
10.Be that as it may, under the provisions of the Act, 2005, the First Appellate
Authority or the State Information Commission can impose penalty and
may also directed for disciplinary action against the Public Information
Officer under Section 20 (2) of the Act, 2005. However, it is pre-condition
that before imposing penalty or passing the order of direction for initiating
departmental proceedings against the Public Information Officer, he is to
be given an opportunity of hearing. The documents placed on recorded
along with the reply filed by the Respondent No. 1/Commission would
show that the Respondent No. 1 has filed a copy of the notice of
complaint as Annexure R-01/01 and further, the copy of the order-sheets
5
dated 25.01.2023 as Annexure R-01/02. On the right-hand side corner, it
is mentioned “issued on 22.08.2023”. Perusal of the order-sheet would
show that in compliance of the order dated 25.01.2023, show-cause
notice under Section 20 (1) and 20 (2) may have been issued on
22.08.2023. 
11.In reply, it is pleaded that the show-cause notice was issued by registered
post. The notice is to be sent on the address of the petitioner who is
posted in the village in rural area. No document has been enclosed to
show that the show-cause notice, if issued on 22.08.2023, was served
upon the petitioner before the date fixed i.e. 22.09.2023.  
12.The order of penalty for failure to provide information is akin to criminal
action to be taken against a person under the law and therefore, it was
the duty cast upon the Commission to record that the notice issued for
imposing penalty and taking disciplinary action is served upon the person
to whom it is issued i.e. the petitioner and even after service of notice, he
failed to appear and submit its reply. In the impugned order dated
22.09.2023, no such finding is recorded by the Respondent No.
1/Commission. In absence of such specific finding recorded by the
Commission before passing an order of imposing penalty under Section
20 (1) of Act, 2005 that the show-cause notice ordered to be issued by the
Commission was issued and served upon the Public Information Officer.
More so, when in the order-sheet pursuant to the order dated 25.01.2023,
the date of issuance is as reflecting only on 22.08.2023 i.e. more than 07
months from the date of order. Service of notice cannot be presumed.
Respondent No. 2 has not filed any document in support of its contention
to show that notice if any, issued by what mode and whether it is served
upon prior to date of hearing. It is mandatory that before imposing penalty
or passing the order of direction for initiating departmental proceedings
6
against the Public Information Officer, he is required to be given an
opportunity of hearing.

13. In the aforementioned facts of the case, as there is no material available
in the record to satisfy that the notice was issued and served upon the
petitioner before the date of hearing of the case. The impugned order
dated 22.09.2023 (Annexure P/1) imposing penalty upon the petitioner
under Section 20 (1) is in violation of principles of natural justice.

14. For the foregoing discussion, order impugned dated 22.09.2023
(Annexure P/1) imposing penalty upon the petitioner is not sustainable in
the eyes of law. Accordingly, it is set-aside. 
15.The writ petition stands allowed.
